## DAILY SECURITY BRIEFING

### 1. European allies deepen military and industrial support for Ukraine
The Coalition of the Willing made air defense an urgent priority and backed greater technology-sharing, sanctions on Russia, and preparations for a multinational force after any credible ceasefire. The EU approved €6.1 billion for air-defense systems, interceptors, ammunition and radars. Britain also authorized the transfer of classified Storm Shadow/SCALP missile information to support production in Ukraine and signed a battlefield-AI partnership with Kyiv.

**Why it matters:** The measures move support beyond weapons deliveries toward integrating Ukraine with European defense production. However, Kyiv still reports a €23 billion defense-budget gap and a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors.

### 2. Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks on economic and military targets
Russia continued attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, including a drone strike on a residential building in Chernihiv that injured at least 20 people. Ukraine reported strikes on Russian logistics facilities, a defense-industrial plant, a fighter aircraft and a mobile Iskander launcher. Kyiv says it needs substantially more funding to expand drone production and match Russia’s strike tempo.

**Why it matters:** Both sides are increasingly targeting logistics, industry and economic resilience rather than only frontline forces. Reciprocal attacks on Black Sea ports and shipping have also sharply disrupted grain exports, with a disproportionate impact on Ukraine’s economy.

### 3. NATO faces growing pressure to counter drone incursions
Supplied reporting describes NATO members increasingly shooting down drones entering their airspace after repeated incidents along the alliance’s eastern flank. European initiatives are focusing on layered defenses using radars, jammers and lower-cost interceptor drones.

**Why it matters:** The incursions create escalation risks while exposing an unfavorable cost exchange when expensive fighter-launched missiles are used against comparatively cheap drones. They are accelerating efforts to build a coordinated European “drone wall.”

### 4. United States launches expanded economic pressure campaign against Iran
Washington sanctioned more than 60 targets and expanded potentially sanctionable sectors, while warning Iran’s trading partners that secondary sanctions could follow within weeks. No deadline or full list of targeted countries was provided. Iran’s rial fell to a record open-market low, while Iranian officials threatened retaliation against states joining the campaign and raised the possibility of disruption around the Strait of Hormuz.

**Why it matters:** Applying secondary sanctions to major Iranian partners—including potentially China, India, Turkey and the UAE—could create wider diplomatic and economic friction. Iranian retaliation could also affect global energy markets and regional security.

## WATCH

- **Storm Shadow production:** Russia says it will identify and attack missile-production facilities in Ukraine; Moscow’s diplomatic confrontation with London is also deepening.
- **Iran sanctions and Hormuz:** Monitor whether Washington names major foreign banks or energy buyers for secondary sanctions and whether Tehran acts on its maritime threats.
- **Israel–Turkey tensions in Syria:** Israel’s strike on a Syrian airbase linked to a suspected Turkish deployment highlights the risk of direct friction; the United States is reportedly pursuing a deconfliction mechanism.

# ASIA Regional Intelligence Briefing

### 1. Taiwan and South China Sea tensions remain closely linked
China continues near-daily military and coast guard activity around Taiwan while maintaining expansive South China Sea claims rejected by a 2016 international arbitration ruling. Recent Chinese drills near the disputed Scarborough Shoal accompanied increasingly frequent confrontations with Philippine and Vietnamese vessels. The United States, United Kingdom and 12 other countries reiterated that Beijing’s broad maritime claims lack a legal basis.

**Why it matters:** A Taiwan crisis could quickly spread into the South China Sea, involving US allies and threatening major shipping routes. Taiwan’s central role in advanced semiconductor production would amplify the global economic consequences of any conflict or blockade.

### 2. US considers additional tariff on Chinese goods
The Trump administration is considering an additional 7.5% tariff on China following a Section 301 investigation into alleged excess industrial capacity and underpriced exports. The measure remains under deliberation and would be added to existing tariffs. Washington reportedly intends to avoid disrupting the one-year trade truce or a planned Trump-Xi meeting.

**Why it matters:** Even a calibrated tariff would renew pressure on US-China economic relations and could affect Asian manufacturing and supply chains. Beijing rejects the overcapacity accusation and favors bilateral negotiations, leaving open the possibility of retaliation or further trade talks.

### 3. China-Russia Arctic shipping cooperation expands
A Chinese container ship reached Murmansk through Russia’s Northern Sea Route for the first time, according to Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom. Chinese operator NewNew Shipping Line plans to deploy additional Arctic-capable vessels, while Chinese firms are considering investments in northern Russian ports.

**Why it matters:** The route could shorten some China-Europe journeys and deepen China-Russia commercial integration. Expanded Arctic shipping would also reduce reliance on routes through the Suez Canal and conflict-exposed Middle Eastern waters, while increasing the strategic importance of Russian-controlled Arctic infrastructure.

## WATCH
- Whether Washington finalizes the proposed China tariff and how Beijing responds ahead of the anticipated Trump-Xi meeting.
- Chinese activity near Scarborough Shoal and Taiwan, particularly any escalation involving Philippine or US forces.

## Europe prioritizes Ukraine’s air defense amid funding shortfall

The Coalition of the Willing pledged to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses, expand defense-industrial cooperation and tighten sanctions on Russia. The EU approved €6.1 billion for air-defense systems, interceptors, ammunition and radars. However, Kyiv says it still faces a €23 billion defense-budget gap, including military pay, weapons procurement and preparations for 2027.

**Why it matters:** Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks are increasing while Ukraine reports severe shortages of Patriot interceptors. The funding gap could constrain military operations and expose cities and infrastructure despite continued European commitments.

## UK transfers missile technology as tensions with Russia deepen

Britain authorized MBDA to share classified information on British components in Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles, supporting eventual assembly or production in Ukraine with French and British participation. London and Kyiv also signed an artificial-intelligence defense partnership based on access to Ukrainian battlefield data. Moscow condemned the missile initiative, threatened to target production facilities and said bilateral relations were at an unprecedented low following the departure of its ambassador from London.

**Why it matters:** Domestic missile production could reduce Ukraine’s dependence on limited Western stockpiles and expand its long-range strike capacity, although production is unlikely to begin quickly. The move also increases the risk of further diplomatic, cyber or military escalation between Russia and the UK.

## Long-range strikes expand economic and regional security risks

Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities, ports, warehouses, transport links and other economic infrastructure, while Ukraine struck Russian logistics facilities, defense-industrial targets and reportedly an Iskander ballistic-missile launcher. Reciprocal attacks around the Black Sea have sharply reduced commercial shipping and Ukrainian grain exports. Separately, repeated drone incursions have prompted NATO states increasingly to intercept unmanned aircraft along the alliance’s eastern flank.

**Why it matters:** The conflict is increasingly targeting each side’s economic resilience and logistics rather than only frontline forces. Disruption to Black Sea trade threatens Ukrainian revenues and international agricultural markets, while drone incidents in NATO airspace raise escalation risks and expose gaps in cost-effective air defense.

## WATCH

- Whether European funding and interceptor deliveries arrive quickly enough to close Ukraine’s air-defense and budget gaps before winter.
- Russian retaliation for UK missile cooperation, and whether drone incursions or Black Sea attacks trigger broader NATO involvement or prolonged shipping disruption.

## 1. US launches expanded economic pressure campaign against Iran

**What happened:** Washington announced sanctions on roughly 60 individuals, companies and vessels linked to Iran and expanded the sectors vulnerable to secondary sanctions to include digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that foreign entities continuing to facilitate Iranian trade or finance could lose access to the US dollar system. Iran’s rial subsequently reached a record-low open-market rate of about 2.02 million to the dollar. Tehran rejected the pressure campaign and threatened consequences for states supporting US economic or military action.

**Why it matters:** The campaign could further weaken Iran’s economy and increase pressure on its major trading partners, particularly China. Enforcement against third countries risks wider financial and diplomatic confrontation. Iranian retaliation against regional energy infrastructure or shipping could also raise oil prices and intensify the existing conflict around the Strait of Hormuz.

## 2. Houthis strike Saudi tanker in the Red Sea

**What happened:** Yemen’s Houthis claimed a ballistic-missile strike on the Saudi-flagged tanker *Amzan* about 63 nautical miles west of Yanbu. Maritime authorities and the vessel’s operator confirmed that a projectile caused a deck fire; all crew were reported safe, with no reported environmental damage. The Houthis said the attack was part of their declared blockade of Saudi-linked shipping.

**Why it matters:** The attack marks a renewed escalation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia and threatens a major route for Saudi oil exports. Disruption in the Red Sea is particularly significant while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is already constrained. Simultaneous pressure on both maritime chokepoints could increase shipping costs, disrupt energy supplies and draw Saudi Arabia deeper into renewed conflict in Yemen.

## 3. Syria emerges as an arena for Israeli-Turkish competition

**What happened:** Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase eight times on 18 August, saying it was pre-empting a Turkish military deployment. Turkey denied that its personnel were present, while Syria said Turkish officers had visited the site shortly before the attack. Israel has previously struck Syrian bases assessed by Turkey as possible deployment locations. Separately, Israeli ground operations reportedly continued in southern Syria despite US-mediated contacts between Israeli and Syrian officials.

**Why it matters:** The incidents demonstrate Syria’s limited control over its airspace and the growing risk of friction between Israel and Turkey, both US partners with major regional military capabilities. Turkish deployments or air-defence systems in Syria could constrain Israeli operations, while further Israeli strikes could undermine efforts to stabilize Syria and establish military deconfliction arrangements.

## WATCH

- **Iran sanctions enforcement and retaliation:** Monitor whether Washington targets Chinese banks or other major Iranian trade partners, and whether Tehran responds against Gulf states, energy facilities or shipping.
- **Gaza ceasefire pressures:** Israeli strikes have continued despite a US request to reduce attacks, while renewed kite and balloon launches could prompt broader Israeli operations.

## U.S.–Canada Trade Dispute Escalates

Canada prepared retaliatory tariffs after trade negotiations with Washington collapsed and the United States imposed or threatened 50% duties on selected Canadian goods. Prime Minister Mark Carney accused Washington of seeking to weaken major Canadian industries, while President Donald Trump threatened additional tariffs on vehicles, auto parts and steel. Ontario Premier Doug Ford also raised the possibility of using electricity and critical-mineral exports as leverage.

**Why it matters:** The dispute threatens deeply integrated North American automotive, steel, agricultural and energy supply chains. Further escalation could raise costs, disrupt production and cause a broader deterioration in relations between the two allies.

## U.S. Resumes Lethal Maritime Counternarcotics Strikes

U.S. Southern Command struck a vessel in the eastern Pacific, killing two people it described as drug traffickers. The command did not publicly provide evidence of the vessel’s involvement in trafficking. The Guardian reported that the wider campaign has killed 223 people in 67 strikes, while Washington is also seeking expanded joint operations against criminal groups in Latin America.

**Why it matters:** The campaign represents an increasingly militarized U.S. approach to regional drug trafficking. Its expansion could generate legal, sovereignty and diplomatic disputes, particularly if operations extend onto partner countries’ territory.

## Colombian Armed Groups Recruit Children for Drone Warfare

Human Rights Watch reported that Colombian rebel and criminal groups are increasingly recruiting children, including through social media, and training some to operate explosives-laden drones. Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ Office recorded 625 child-recruitment cases in 2024 and reported 121 drone attacks in the first five months of the current year, killing 21 people and injuring 145.

**Why it matters:** The trend indicates renewed armed-group activity in areas left vulnerable after the 2016 FARC peace agreement. The use of children and weaponized drones complicates Colombia’s security response and increases risks to civilians, police and military facilities.

## WATCH

- **Canadian retaliation:** The scale and targeting of Ottawa’s tariffs, and whether provinces restrict electricity or critical-mineral exports to the United States.
- **Expansion of U.S. counternarcotics operations:** Whether Latin American governments authorize land-based joint missions and how regional states respond to further lethal strikes.

articles.title: How close are Russia and the UK to war?
articles.body:
How close are Russia and the UK to war?
Russia just pulled its ambassador to the UK, as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham doubles down on open involvement in the Ukraine conflict. The risk of open war has never been higher, but Burnham is writing checks that he can’t cash.
Relations between Russia and the UK are at an “unprecedentedly low level,” Moscow’s embassy in London said in a statement on Sunday, after it emerged that ambassador Andrey Kelin had left his post in late July and would not be immediately replaced. In a follow-up statement to the Sunday Times, an embassy spokesperson said that Kelin had made “considerable efforts to preserve contacts and channels of communication” between the UK and Russia, but the UK had clearly chosen a “path of confrontation.”
☝️ Russia-UK relations across all areas have deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London's initiative.https://t.co/ddib4uE1B4pic.twitter.com/BrdJAyk4bO
— Russian Embassy, UK (@RussianEmbassy) August 23, 2026
“He left Britain in the hope that a more constructive and respectful dialogue could eventually be restored, should the UK reconsider its policies towards our country,” the spokesman added.
How did Russia/UK relations get this bad?
Well, firstly, Keir Starmer, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson, Theresa May, and of course David Cameron and their anglophonic media bullhorns.
Moscow has viewed the UK as one of Ukraine’s most bellicose foreign backers since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022. Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson intervened to scupper a peace deal between Moscow and Kiev that April; Britain supplied Ukraine with ‘Storm Shadow’ cruise missiles for long-range strikes on Russia a year later; and in the latest revelation by the British press, Ukraine utilized a plethora of British-made drones in its campaign of long-range attacks on Russian civilian targets this year.
On August 17, the Russian embassy in London warned Britain that “the deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov added that Moscow has “every right to regard the proudly proclaimed direct involvement of British missile forces in strikes against Russia as participation in the war, with all the consequences that entails.”
Neither statement seems to have deterred Burnham. Later that day, the British PM proclaimed that the UK would continue “to support Ukraine 100%.” Six days later, his office announced that it would provide Ukraine with classified information enabling it to produce Storm Shadow cruise missiles on Ukrainian soil. Burnham followed this up with a visit to Kiev on Monday, where he compared the conflict to Britain’s struggle against Nazi Germany in World War II, and promised to supply Ukraine with anti-air missiles to repel Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Is pulling the ambassador a sign of war?
The withdrawal of Kelin is an unprecedented move. Diplomatic relations between Moscow and London have been strained on multiple occasions during the post-Soviet period, Russia’s response has typically been restrained. When FSB agents caught British spies hiding a listening device outside the Russian embassy in 2006, the Kremlin named and condemned the agents responsible. When the UK expelled four Russian diplomats after Moscow refused to extradite a suspect in the alleged poisoning of double agent Alexander Litvinenko in 2007, Russia responded in kind.
Similarly, when the UK expelled 23 diplomats in 2018 over the alleged poisoning of undercover MI6 agent Sergei Skripal, Moscow’s response was the tit-for-tat expulsion of 23 Brits staff and the closure of a British consulate-general in St. Petersburg.
At no point during these incidents did Russia withdraw – or threaten to withdraw – its ambassador. However, with relations already in the gutter since 2022, Moscow’s lack of urgency in replacing Kelin most likely does not herald military action against the UK. Instead, it is an acknowledgement of just how badly relations have deteriorated.
What will Russia do to neutralize the UK’s Ukraine missile threat?
Russia’s kinetic response to Burnham’s missile data sharing plan is straightforward. In a statement to reporters on August 24, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that “our armed forces are carrying out the relevant work and obtaining the necessary data in order to identify the production sites for such missiles and other military equipment, and are taking measures to destroy these locations.”
Destroying missile production sites in Ukraine is a far easier task for Russia now than at any point since 2022. Ukraine has no ammunition for its Patriot air defense batteries left, nor does Kiev have any money to buy more. In a post on X on Sunday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky admitted that his military used all of its 2026 budget in the first six months of the year buying and building drones to attack civilian infrastructure in Russia.
As a result, Russia has been dismantling weapons plants, ports and ships used to import arms, and energy targets across Ukraine with impunity since July.
How far can Britain escalate against Russia?
Burnham has little more to offer. The US is unwilling to share its dwindling stocks of Patriot missiles with Ukraine, even if the UK offers to buy. Three out of five weapons packages donated by the UK to Ukraine this year included other models of defense missiles – a total of more than 2,500 missiles – but these have apparently been used up by Kiev’s forces.
Britain’s ability to escalate beyond data-sharing and weapons packages is constrained by two key factors. Firstly, open UK intervention in Ukraine could trigger a cataclysmic, and likely nuclear, conflict between Russia and NATO. Secondly, Britain’s armed forces have been hollowed out by decades of underfunding: there are fewer active-duty troops in the British military than at any point since the end of the Napoleonic Wars; Britain reportedly has enough ammunition for less than a day of full-scale combat; and no means of defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Given the potential consequences, some figures within the British defense establishment have called for restraint. Former Chief of the Defense Staff Tony Radakin – who once urged Britain to prepare to fight Russia in space – and his successor, Richard Knighton, have both reportedly sought contact with Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov in order to limit the threat of naval escalation. Another former British defense chief, Field Marshal Lord David Richards, has called for peace talks with Russia since 2022, arguing last year that Ukraine “cannot win” the conflict with anything short of full-scale NATO intervention.
Even former defense attache John Foreman – who has encouraged Ukraine to strike Russia with British-made missiles – told The Times on August 15 that Britain should reopen “strategic dialog” with Russia, calling London’s suspension of military-to-military communications in 2024 “daft.”
'Good to speak to @edvaizey today about the need to hold our noses and re-establish mil to mil ties.
We can continue to support Ukraine. But at the same time, we can talk to the Russians'. Cutting military communication with Russia was a 'daft decision'.
With Russian forces…
These calls have also come from the UK’s typically hawkish circuit of ‘Russia experts’. Among this group is Mark Galeotti, an academic with rumored links to British intelligence. In an interview with former British diplomat Ian Proud in mid-August, Galeotti conceded that “behind closed doors,” many British diplomatic and security officials now believe that “we’ve reached the stage where we need to be pushing both sides to some kind of resolution.”
“After years of spouting these empty mantras of ‘as much as it takes, for as long as it takes’, etc etc, who’s going to turn around and say ‘actually, come to think of it, this is not in our interests’,” he told Proud.
Will Burnham step back?
Burnham, Galeotti argued, is unlikely to spend precious political capital on restarting diplomacy with Russia, as to do so would open him up to attacks from rival parties and hawks within his own Labour Party.
After his speech in Kiev on Monday, Burnham chaired a meeting of the ‘coalition of the willing’ – a 34-nation group put together to pool military aid for Ukraine. In his opening remarks, Burnham called on the UK’s allies to “dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks” to keep the Ukrainian military fighting.
However, should the UK continue supplying long-range missiles and drones to Ukraine, and should these munitions be used to kill Russian civilians, Russia is running out of diplomatic means of deterring London.
Britain has scoffed at every polite warning from Moscow to date, but with Kelin’s office vacant, there are fewer civilized options available to Russia. The “consequences” threatened by Lavrov could be far more catastrophic than a formal demarche.

articles.title: Ukraine Allies Defy Moscow Threats, Pledge Air Defense Boost and Missile Production
articles.body:
Ukraine’s allies on Monday pledged to keep up their support amid Russia’s escalating attacks and despite threats from Moscow, as they gathered in Kyiv on Ukraine’s Independence Day.
Air defense supplies were the main priority at the meeting of 30 leaders of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, jointly chaired by the leaders of France and Germany, who participated remotely, and by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first trip abroad since taking office, alongside other European leaders and European Council President António Costa.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine’s defense,” Burnham said.
Russia has recently pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles, ripping open apartment blocks and killing dozens in the capital.
The escalating Russian strikes have pushed civilian deaths to their highest levels since the first months of Moscow’s 2022 invasion.
A Russian drone attack on Chernihiv, north of the capital, wounded 15 people, Ukraine’s emergency services said, while one person was killed and nine wounded in shelling on Izyum in the east, according to local authorities.
“Right now, things are really very difficult for all of us. But there is a force holding us firmly by the hand,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an address, adding: “It is the strength of our mutual circle.”
Kellogg Backs Mobilization of Ukrainian Women
Zelensky later told the assembled leaders in an evening address that he wanted to “raise production” of drones and missiles to wage “more attacks” on Russia, matching its strikes on Ukraine.
For that, “we need more money – much more,” he said.
Burnham told the allies that “the clear message to Putin should be that Ukraine will never give up territory that Russia cannot win on the battlefield, and negotiations must start from the line of contact.”
French President Emmanuel Macron warned that “Russia will try to escalate against European countries in order to deter them from assisting Ukraine.”
“It’s clear that NATO countries will be targeted and the provocations will multiply,” he added.
EU releases €6.1 billion for Ukraine’s defense
The European Union said Monday it had released another €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defenses.
The funding is part of a €90-billion loan, including €60 billion in military aid, that the EU has said will go to Ukraine.
Ahead of the talks, Ukraine forged ahead with its campaign against Russia’s logistics sites, hitting multiple warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early Monday at two warehouses in southern Russia, adding that two other sites had been evacuated over threats of drone attacks.
Russian authorities also said debris from a Ukrainian drone attack had killed three children and wounded eight others.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Saturday said Kyiv had “opened Pandora’s box” by targeting Russia’s economy and promised further escalation, including against Ukrainian agriculture.
UK clears Storm Shadow technology transfer
Burnham announced in Kyiv that the British government was authorizing defense firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range Storm Shadow/SCALP missile.
The Kremlin accused London of preventing peace in Ukraine by handing the information to Kyiv and threatened to target and “destroy” facilities producing the missile in Ukraine.
On Saturday, Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.
The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult for Kyiv to intercept.
Ukraine relies on advanced systems – chiefly, US Patriot interceptors – to protect its skies.
But it has reported a shortage of Patriot interceptors since the United States and Israel went to war with Iran in February, diverting supplies.
Ukraine reveals scale of Patriot shortfall
Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.
He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
“Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased,” Zelensky said.
“For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264,” he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.

articles.title: Burnham ups the ante in fight against Russia — and leaves Merz in the shade
articles.body:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham poses in front the Wall of Remembrance at Mykhailivska Square in Kyiv on Aug. 24, 2026. | Pool photo by Henry Nicholls via WPA/Getty Images
LONDON — Andy Burnham has deepened Britain’s support for Ukraine by boosting the war-torn country’s ability to develop long-range missiles, in his first major move on foreign policy since becoming prime minister.
To mark the PM’s visit to Ukraine — his first overseas trip since taking office last month —Downing Street announced that the U.K. government will allow European defense company MBDA to declassify information about British-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles in order to help Ukraine build its own version.
The missile initiative puts pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who had called for German-Swedish Taurus cruise missiles to be given to Ukraine while he was in opposition, only to backtrack after taking office — and who opted out of attending independence day festivities in Kyiv on Monday.
Advertisement
The trip gave Burnham his first chance to show his commitment to the Coalition of the Willing — a grouping of Ukraine’s allies championed by his predecessor, Keir Starmer — as he co-chaired its latest meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron.
Burnham was allowed to enjoy the limelight as the only E3 leader to attend the session in person, with Macron hosting Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman and Merz attending to a domestic crisis.
Sitting alongside Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Burnham said Russian threats against the U.K. will not deter him and show British assistance is having an impact.
The British PM said: “It’s clear Russia is running out of options so Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.”
The new agreement on missiles is unlikely to have any short-term impact on Russia’s war against Ukraine, but represents a gradual shift in the U.K.’s posture towards deeper cooperation with Kyiv and sharper confrontation with Moscow.
Burnham has also signed a deal allowing the U.K. to access Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab, allowing both sides to collaborate on the development of new battlefield technology, using sensors and cameras to capture and collate information on objects such as tanks, artillery, air defense systems and drone targets.
Advertisement
Speaking in front of St. Sofia Cathedral in Kyiv to mark the 35th anniversary of the nation’s independence, Burnham said: “This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war.”
He vowed that “despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country we will continue our support for Ukraine.”
Turning up the temperature
Germany’s Merz is facing fresh criticism of his stance from within his own parliamentary group, from his coalition partner, and from the opposition. “It’s a clear sign that both countries are no longer waiting for Germany or relying on Germany in this matter,” CDU/CSU foreign policy politician Roderich Kiesewetter told POLITICO.
He added that the British-French initiative was “a call to Germany that, unfortunately, will once again have no effect and also highlights our limited credibility.”
Merz most recently justified his refusal to supply Taurus missiles during a government question session in the Bundestag in March, stating that his support for the idea, expressed while he was in the opposition, had been made “in a different context” — specifically, when Germany had more Taurus missiles for its own defense.
Yet the move comes at a particularly fraught moment for British relations with Russia, after The Times reports that Moscow has withdrawn its ambassador in London without appointing a replacement.
Advertisement
Asked about the decision on British missile technology, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused Britain of “methodically and regularly adding fuel to the fire and methodically and regularly plotting to prevent any progress in the peace process.”
Al Carns, a Labour MP who resigned as U.K. armed forces minister earlier this summer over defense funding, told POLITICO the announcement is “a welcome step forward” but should not be seen as an “escalation.” He suggested it is the equivalent of Iran sharing drone technology with Russia.
John Foreman, a former U.K. defense attaché to Russia and Ukraine, said it was “an evolution of position worked out over many months” and “will give Ukraine another string to its bow” at a time when the U.S. is not providing assistance with long-range missiles.
He added: “It shows we won’t be bullied by Russian threats and bluster nor deterred from supporting Ukraine now and in the future.”
A Ukrainian official, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, hailed Burnham’s show of solidarity as “very significant,” backed up by “a great deliverable.”
The prime minister’s spokesman declined to say the U.K. is adopting a tougher posture, telling journalists: “Our position in support of Ukraine has always been clear. We have invested billions of pounds into helping them win the fight against Russia. We’ve cracked down on Russia in terms of economic sanctions, and that this is a continuation of that stance.”
Advertisement
Words or actions?
The U.K.’s latest announcement has been in train for several months, according to two people with knowledge of the process, and will run alongside Operation Brakestop — the U.K.’s project with Ukraine to develop low-cost long-range strike weapons.
U.K. officials played down any heightened risk of retaliation with Russia, with one senior Whitehall figure, also granted anonymity to speak freely, saying that Moscow’s words did not appear to be matched by any tangible change in their actions.
Matthew Savill, director of military sciences at RUSI, said: “The Russians would almost certainly want to try and locate and destroy any such factory [producing advanced missiles,] but this is hardly an escalation given that SCALP and Storm Shadow were launched at targets inside Russia two years ago, and other Western companies are already assisting with repair and production inside Ukraine.”
This article has been updated. Dan Bloom and Hans von der Burchard contributed reporting.

articles.title: The Guardian view on Britain helping Ukraine: build the weapons independence Kyiv needs | Editorial
articles.body:
The events of the past few days on Europe’s borders may mark a turning point in Russia’s war on Ukraine. While the political skies in Kyiv have darkened for Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the military picture looks brighter. Ukraine can already send swarms of drones against Russian oil facilities, e-commerce warehouses and airfields. Andy Burnham’s arrival in Kyiv marks a step forward. Britain is releasing classified information on its components of Scalp, the French version of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow cruise missile, enabling its assembly in Ukraine. This is more than another weapon for Kyiv. Britain is helping Ukraine become less dependent on the western armoury.
Moscow sabre-rattles, but Britain should hold its nerve. Kyiv has been at the mercy of its allies, waiting to replenish weapons stockpiles and release sophisticated arms. Producing its own hi-tech armoury gives Ukraine greater freedom of action because western governments have let go. Two years ago it was different. Joe Biden waited until November 2024 before letting Ukraine strike deep into Russia with US weapons. Yet thresholds once deemed dangerously escalatory have since been crossed without provoking a Russia-Nato war. Kyiv is now being trusted with something more consequential: a measure of weapons independence.
It needs this. Ukraine cannot overcome its manpower disadvantage by fighting Russia soldier for soldier for every kilometre of its vital eastern fortress belt, where Kyiv is losing ground. If Moscow can freely push ammunition, drones and equipment towards Donetsk, eventually something will give. Cruise missiles offer another strategy, making it harder and costlier for Russian forces to reach the front. Europe is thinking defensively too. Ukraine relies heavily on the US-made Patriots to down ballistic missiles, but global shortages of interceptors, a situation made worse by the US war with Iran, have left it exposed. With European help, Ukraine’s defence industry is developing an anti-ballistic system intended to reduce that dependence. Kyiv is ramping up its own ballistic missiles. If both are successful, Ukraine would be better able both to strike and defend itself without first appealing to Washington.
War is a terrible thing, but what is the alternative? Moscow offers little evidence that territorial success would satisfy it. Despite enormous casualties and painfully slow advances, Vladimir Putin rejects proposals that fail to meet Russia’s broader conditions while expanding military power rather than preparing his people for compromise. Then there is the rise of the far right in Europe, large parts of which are pro-Russia. If Mr Putin thinks that the outlook for Russia’s position will improve politically over the next two or three years, he will bargain harder. Why accept merely the Donbas today if the coalition supporting Ukraine might be weaker tomorrow? That option disappears if either Russia’s war burden becomes intolerable or the west convincingly insulates its material help from political change.
History offers lessons. In Vladislav M Zubok’s Collapse: The Fall of the Soviet Union, Boris Yeltsin is startled to hear that Ukrainians, including millions of Russian speakers, want independence in 1991. Once convinced this is their democratic will, however, he accepts it. Russia, he says, will “recognise this new political reality”. Mr Putin starts from the same sense of historical intimacy and reaches the opposite conclusion: that Ukraine’s democratic choices cannot override Russia’s claim to a privileged role in its future. That is a revanchist error he ought to regret.

articles.title: How Syria's skies are becoming a new Israel-Turkey battleground
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Syria's skies are becoming a new Israel-Turkey battleground
On 18 August, Israeli fighter jets struck a northwestern Syrian airfield eight times, with Tel Aviv claiming it had pre-empted a Turkish military deployment there.
While the raid did not result in a clash between the two powerful militaries, it nevertheless demonstrated once again how Syria essentially has no control over its airspace.
The airstrikes hit Syria’s Abu al-Duhur Air Base, causing damage but no casualties. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani said that Turkish military officers visited the site days before the strike. Turkey denied that any delegation was at the base before or during the attack.
Israel claimed Turkey was “on the verge of breaching” the “status quo in security matters” by deploying troops, with Ankara, in turn, describing Israel’s actions as an “unacceptable” and “reckless” threat to regional peace and stability.
Israel previously bombed three airbases in central Syria in April 2025 shortly after Turkey scoped them for potentially deploying forces.
All of these incidents highlight how Syria’s airspace, far from being under its sovereign control, is being contested by its two powerful neighbours who both have large American-equipped air forces.
While Israel appears predominant for now, Turkey may seek to incrementally put constraints on its rival’s aerial supremacy over its southern neighbour.
The battle over Syria's airspace
“The pressure on Israel’s freedom of action in Syria appears to be increasing, even if it has not yet produced a decisive constraint,” Muaz Al Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the non-profit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, told The New Arab.
He noted that the Trump administration has signalled an effort to broaden the Abraham Accords to include Syria “while reducing the scope of conflicts” involving Israel, and the US by extension, in the Middle East. “That diplomatic backdrop coincides with a visible change on the ground,” Abdullah said.
ACLED data shows a notable decline in Israeli airstrikes in Syria since August 2025. Abdullah assesses that this might mean the “operational window” Israel enjoyed since the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad collapsed in December 2024 is beginning to narrow.
“The broader picture, however, is more mixed: Israeli incursions and violence against civilians have continued in uneven but persistent patterns,” Abdullah told The New Arab.
“The shift suggests that Israel may be relying more heavily on ground incursions and other forms of pressure to meet its immediate security objectives,” he added.
“Airstrikes, by contrast, appear to be reserved for moments when those measures are deemed insufficient, as reflected in strikes against Abu al-Duhur, T4, Tadmor, and Hama airbases.”
Replacing Russia's role?
Before the dramatic, free-fall collapse of the brutal Assad regime, Russia officially controlled much of Syria’s airspace around regime-controlled areas and bombed opposition-held regions like Idlib.
Shortly after Russia intervened in Syria’s civil war in September 2015, it established a deconfliction mechanism with Israel, allowing the Israeli Air Force to continue striking suspected Iranian assets in the war-torn country.
US Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said after Israel’s latest strike that the US is working on a similar mechanism between Israel, Turkey, and Syria to reduce the risk of clashes.
Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, doesn’t believe this necessarily indicates that Turkey is replacing Russia’s pre-2024 role in Syria or will ever replace it.
“Unlike Russia, Turkey, at least for now, does not appear capable of deterring Israel from carrying out military incursions and strikes inside Syria,” Ozeren told The New Arab.
“Israel’s decision to bomb Abu al-Duhur Air Base, located relatively close to the Turkish-Syrian border, sends a clear message to both the (Syrian President Ahmed) al-Sharaa government and Ankara,” he added.
“Although Turkey responded to the incident with a relatively restrained protest, the strike itself is a troubling indication of how quickly tensions between Israel and Turkey could escalate.”
Deconfliction and de-escalation
Kristin Ronzi, a Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, says the Turkish-Israeli deconfliction mechanism has already helped de-escalate tensions between the two countries in Syria and “mitigate the risk” of miscalculation.
“As such, Turkey has maintained significant influence over Syrian airspace in the north, while Israel has influence in the south,” Ronzi told The New Arab.
“Even so, the early 18 August Israeli airstrikes against Abu al-Duhur military base in northwestern Syria indicate that Israel is able to extend its operations further into Syria.”
She noted that Barrack’s description of the Israeli strikes as “unnecessary escalation” indicates a limited US tolerance for Israeli airstrikes in Syria in light of warming US-Syria ties and concerns over “Turkish-Israeli frictions”.
“The Trump administration will likely tolerate Israel’s military presence in southern Syria and sporadic ground incursions,” Ronzi said. “But the United States will likely pressure Israel to restrict airstrikes, especially against targets that do not pose a national security threat and risk elevating Syrian-Israeli tensions,” the analyst added.
“Syria will rhetorically reject Israeli violations of its airspace; Syria will be unwilling and unable to effectively control its airspace.”
ACLED’s Abdullah expects that the present status quo of Israel dominating Syria’s southern and central airspace without “direct contestation” with Turkey in central Syria, where there are overlapping areas of influence, will hold.
He recalled Israel’s airstrikes against central Syrian airbases in April 2025 to deter Turkey from establishing any presence.
“The recent strike on Abu al-Duhur does not necessarily represent a contest for dominance between Israel and Turkey in northern Syria,” he said. “It is better understood as a matter of undeclared areas of influence between the two sides, alongside Israeli political objectives tied to the domestic situation inside Israel,” Abdullah added.
“At the same time, where Turkish and Israeli influence in Syria begins and ends is a separate question from Israel’s deterrence strategy of preventing Syria from acquiring an effective, modern air force. That strategy is also one of the reasons behind the Abu al-Duhur strike.”
Ronzi believes Israel will likely reject any Turkish efforts to expand its military influence any further in central Syria.
“Efforts to enhance Syria’s air defence systems would likely be a red line for Israel and Israel would likely obstruct any such efforts, including potentially through pre-emptive airstrikes as Israel has previously done,” she said.
Dreams of a new Syrian air force
Israel’s post-Assad airstrikes destroyed much of what was left of the old regime’s Russian-built air defences and antiquated air force, including its most advanced fighter jets, the Soviet-era MiG-29.
Syria still has some less advanced flyable jets, including Czech-built L-39 light attack aircraft, two of which performed a flyby in a July graduation ceremony for air force cadets, and vintage Soviet-era Su-22s, two of which were spotted over Idlib this August. Israel opposes Syria reconstituting its air force and air defence.
Israel was even concerned that the installation of an HTRS-100 Air Traffic Control Radar System built by Turkey’s Aselsan at Damascus International Airport in January could challenge its air supremacy over Syria.
Ronzi noted that while the HTRS-100 has “commercial and civilian benefits,” it nonetheless “raised Israeli concerns” that it could constrain its military operations.
While Turkey might be able to support “limited Syrian air defence infrastructure,” Abdullah predicts that Israel is likely to “draw a clear line” around any capability that could give Damascus any “meaningful independent control” over its skies.
“Israel’s defence doctrine has increasingly rested on keeping neighbouring states unable to threaten it militarily,” he said.
“In that context, Israel may tolerate Turkey’s deployment of the HTRS-100 radar system at Damascus International Airport, but it is expected to resist any further steps that would allow Syrian forces to own or operate effective air capabilities.”
Ozeren noted that maintaining control over Syrian airspace remains a “key security objective” for Israel that increasingly conflicts with Turkey’s ambitions to expand its influence and presence on the ground in that country.
“Syrian airspace, therefore, is likely to become a major arena in which the competing objectives of Israel and Turkey are tested,” he said. “Without meaningful US intervention, tensions between Israel and Turkey could escalate further.”
“If this competition becomes prolonged, Damascus may eventually seek a more formidable external partner capable of balancing these pressures,” he added. “In that context, a renewed reliance on Russia, though seemingly implausible today, could become a more viable option in the near future.”
ACLED’s Abdullah anticipates that Damascus is likely to turn to Ankara for help in any attempt to rebuild the country’s air force. The expanding partnership between the two makes such cooperation plausible. Turkey could provide pilot training, aircraft, and technical support.
“Recent developments suggest that Syria is already preparing for that possibility,” he said. “The graduation of more than 1,000 non-commissioned officers from the Syrian Air Force Academy points to a broader effort to restore the country’s air arm.”
However, what type of aircraft Syria might seek from Turkey remains uncertain. Furthermore, any procurement decision Damascus ultimately makes will likely be shaped by financial constraints and red lines imposed by Israel.
“Syria may also choose to invest more heavily in unmanned systems rather than trying to rebuild a conventional fighter fleet from the ground up,” Abdullah told The New Arab. “Turkey has a clear advantage in drones, and Syrian forces already have experience that Ankara could help develop,” he added.
“Such a strategy would allow Damascus to challenge Israeli dominance indirectly, without attempting to match Israel in the manned-fighter arena.”
RANE’s Ronzi recalled that Israel’s ferocious attacks on weapons caches and the remnants of Assad’s military following the regime collapse significantly degraded any new military threat his successor can pose to Israel.
“Rebuilding the Syrian Air Force is not likely to be a near-term priority for the interim Syrian government as it faces numerous domestic threats, including the Islamic State, as well as the task of developing new state institutions, over time,” Ronzi said.
Syria will probably attempt to buy new aircraft to improve its military capabilities, most likely from Turkey.
“Even though Israel would maintain a qualitative military edge over any Syrian air force, Israel will be wary of any Syrian effort to rebuild its air force and concerned about the potential that it could eventually be used against Israel,” Ronzi added.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in the Middle East who writes extensively about the region's affairs, conflicts, and politics
Follow him on Twitter: @pauliddon

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian drone strikes residential building in central Chernihiv, injuring at least 20, including 3 children
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russian drone strikes residential building in central Chernihiv, injuring at least 20, including 3 children
Key developments on Aug. 24:
- Russian drone strikes residential building in central Chernihiv, injuring at least 20, including 3 children, on Ukraine's Independence Day
- Ukraine hits Ozon logistics centers, rocket fuel plant, MiG-29 fighter jet in Russia, military says
- Russia reacts to UK sharing Storm Shadow blueprints with Ukraine
- 10 Ukrainian soldiers believed missing return home from Russian captivity in 'special exchange'
- EU greenlights $7 billion in defense loans on Ukraine Independence Day
A Russian drone struck an apartment building in central Chernihiv on Aug. 24, injuring at least 20 people, including three children, and sparking a fire, local authorities said.
The Chernihiv City Council said Russian forces launched three waves of attacks on the city, with a drone striking a residential building during the final wave around noon local time.
Police bomb disposal officers said the attack may have involved a jet-powered Geran-5 drone, according to Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus.
"Cynical strike by Russian terrorists on a residential building in Chernihiv. Right in the middle of the day — on Independence Day," Chaus said.
A fire broke out on the ground floor of a nine-story residential building, Ukraine's Emergency Service said.
read also
Ukraine hits Ozon logistics centers, rocket fuel plant, MiG-29 fighter jet in Russia, military says
Ukraine launched a large-scale overnight attack on Russia on Aug. 24, striking Ozon logistics centers, the Kombinat Kamenskiy defense-industrial facility, and a MiG-29 fighter jet, among other targets, the Ukrainian military said.
Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, confirmed that the Ukrainian overnight attack hit Ozon facilities, but did not specify their location or how many were struck.
Three Ozon warehouses were hit in Dagestan, Stavropol Krai and Adygea, Russian independent media outlet Astra reported. Ozon shares fell 12% following the Ukrainian strikes, according to the report.
Murat Kumpilov, head of Russia's Adygea republic, confirmed that the Ozon warehouse caught fire following the attack and that its employees were evacuated. No one was injured, Kumpilov said.
Acting head of Dagestan Fyodor Shchukin said debris from downed drones sparked a fire at a warehouse. He did not specify which company operates the facility. Two warehouse employees were injured in the attack, Shchukin added.
Stavropol Krai Governor Vladimir Vladimirov also confirmed that Ukrainian drones attacked the city of Nevinnomyssk's industrial area, without saying what sites were targeted.
read also
Russia reacts to UK sharing Storm Shadow blueprints with Ukraine
The Kremlin condemned Britain's decision to share classified technical information on Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles with Ukraine, calling the move "fuel on the fire," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Aug. 24.
London has agreed to let European defense company MBDA share classified technical information on British-made components in SCALP cruise missiles with Ukraine, a move that could help Kyiv expand domestic production of the weapons.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to formally announce the decision during his first visit to Kyiv since taking office.
Peskov said Moscow views the decision "extremely negatively," accusing London of doing everything possible "to prevent any progress in the peace process."
Peskov also claimed Russian forces were already gathering information on potential production sites for the missiles and other military equipment in order to target them.
The recent move builds on the U.K.'s 2023 decision to become the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range strike weapons for defensive purposes. It will pave the way for French-Ukrainian assembly of the missiles in Ukraine, while access to the blueprints could bring Kyiv and Paris closer to establishing local production lines, the U.K. government said on Aug. 24.
read also
10 Ukrainian soldiers believed missing return home from Russian captivity in 'special exchange'
Ukraine brought home 10 service members previously considered missing in action from Russian captivity in a "special exchange" via Belarus on Aug. 24, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced, as Ukraine marked its Independence Day.
The service members served in the Ukrainian Armed Forces and National Guard and fought on the Donetsk sector of the front line, Zelensky said.
Two had been considered missing since 2024, while the other eight had been missing since 2025, Ukraine's Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said. The group included sergeants, soldiers and sailors, Lubinets added.
"It is very important that we managed to bring them back," Zelensky said.
"We remember every man and woman who remains in captivity. We are searching for every name. And we will do everything to free them and bring them home," he added.
read also
EU greenlights $7 billion in defense loans on Ukraine Independence Day
Ukraine will receive 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) in defense loans to be spent on air defenses, missiles, ammunition, and radars, according to an Aug. 24 press release from the European Commission.
All the money being disbursed comes from the 90 billion euro ($105 billion) Ukraine Support Loan, which the bloc finalized in April to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's defense and budgetary needs until the end of 2027.
"On Ukraine's Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in the press release.
"As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine, and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it."
The European bloc has emerged as Kyiv's leading military supplier and partner as the Trump administration ended nearly all U.S. defense aid to the war-torn country.

articles.title: Burnham’s visit to Kyiv marks a renewal of badly needed support for Ukraine
articles.body:
Since moving into Downing Street in July, Andy Burnham – a foreign policy neophyte – has expressed strong support for Ukraine. But on Monday he saw the bitter human cost of the war up close for the first time, visiting Kyiv during his first international trip as prime minister.
The occasion was the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave awards to the families of fallen soldiers. Relatives wept, hugging Ukraine’s president. Photos of young men in their prime were shown on a giant screen.
The setting was St Sophia cathedral in the old heart of the Ukrainian capital. Built in the 11th century, the building predates Moscow and is a symbol of Ukraine’s ancient statehood. Next to it were modern weapons used by Kyiv in its struggle against Russia, including quadcopter drones and unmanned land robots.
In a speech in front of other western leaders, Burnham compared Ukraine’s fight to that waged by Britain during the darkest days of the second world war. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” he declared.
Like other high-profile visitors, Burnham arrived with a gift. Since 2023 the UK and France have been providing Kyiv with long-range Storm Shadow or Scalp (as the French version is known) cruise missiles, used to knock out Russian naval ships and command centres.
It was now handing over British blueprints for key components, Burnham said, so Ukraine could eventually make its own version with France.
More Storm Shadows could go some way to dealing with Ukraine’s biggest problem: the wave of ballistic missiles fired by Russia that rain down on Kyiv and other cities most nights. As of now, Ukraine has run out of US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting them down. The Trump administration is disinclined to provide more.
The British cruise missiles carry a larger payload than the long-range drones favoured by Kyiv. They could be used to destroy enemy ballistic missile launch systems, which can be quickly moved, and are dotted around sites in western Russia. Depending on their range, they could also disable military runways and aerodromes.
But nobody expects production to start soon. In the meantime, the Kremlin has responded with characteristic belligerence. Vladimir Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow would destroy any Ukrainian Storm Shadow factories, and accused London of taking part in the war and adding “fuel to the fire” though it is France that is helping with building them.
Last week Russia threatened “consequences” over the supply of British drones to Kyiv and withdrew its ambassador from London. It is unclear how Putin might escalate further. He has already sent assassins to poison Russian dissidents on UK territory including the murder in 2006 of Alexander Litvinenko, killed with radioactive tea.
Burnham appears unmoved by what he dubbed “outrageous” Russian threats, an encouraging sign for Kyiv. On Monday he pointed out that it was Putin who “started the fire” with his illegal and unprovoked invasion, and assured Zelenskyy of his “personal commitment” to Kyiv’s existential cause.
Ukraine has warmly welcomed the Storm Shadow initiative. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, told the Guardian he hoped manufacturing could begin in “months, not years”. “We have proved many times we can do impossible things in producing weaponry,” he said, adding that the missile strengthened Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Moscow.
Of Burnham’s visit, he added: “For us, it’s hugely symbolic and important. It illustrates that for the UK Ukraine remains a top priority. You are an important bridge and have rectified the situation whenever we have a crisis in our relations with the US. Your king is a valuable diplomatic tool and puts in a good word for us with Trump.”
The trip also signalled to allies that the UK will continue to play a leading role in the coalition of the willing after the departure of Keir Starmer. Co-hosting a coalition meeting for the first time, Burnham said Europe would do everything it could to source more Patriotic interceptors for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has asked for 300 to help the country survive the coming winter.
Burnham’s speech made clear that he regards Ukraine’s struggle as Britain’s too – at a time when the US has in effect given up on its attempts to broker a peace deal, and has halted direct military aid. “Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security but the frontline in keeping Europe safe,” he said. “The Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support but our gratitude and respect.”
Ukrainian leaders and soldiers are grateful for British diplomatic and moral support, though they know that London’s military power is limited. Storm Shadow is deemed to have been one of the UK’s most useful contributions but stockpiles were modest.
Ukraine’s focus has been on developing its own long-range drones and cruise missiles, such as Fire Point’s Flamingo, which have been used to strike refineries and warehouses deep inside Russia. The goal is to attack Russia with 1,000 drones and some missiles a day this year, not when Storm Shadow production lines are ready.
But the deal that Burnham has agreed with Zelenskyy is an important renewal of goodwill. At some point Zelenskyy will probably need the help of European allies whenever the White House re-engages with the peace process. Burnham may become an important interlocutor with Trump, and today’s trip is from Ukraine’s perspective an encouraging start.
- 
  Betrayal by Luke Harding (Guardian Faber, £20) is published on Thursday. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

articles.title: Ukraine Lands Rare Hit on Mobile Iskander Launcher Used for Ballistic Missile Strikes
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Lands Rare Hit on Mobile Iskander Launcher Used for Ballistic Missile Strikes
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Iskander ballistic missile launcher near the border in a rare and potentially significant operation aimed at destroying Moscow’s missile systems before they can fire, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, Ukrinform reported on August 23.
The strike comes at a particularly critical moment for Ukraine as supplies of interceptor missiles for its Patriot air defense systems remain under severe pressure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia has increasingly relied on ballistic missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, and the threat is becoming more acute as another winter approaches. Patriot remains one of Ukraine’s most important defenses against such weapons, which descend toward their targets at extremely high speeds and are far harder to intercept than conventional cruise missiles or drones.
With interceptor stocks limited, however, Ukraine is increasingly seeking another solution: destroying the launchers themselves.
“Today we have another success. We can’t give many details due to the sensitivity of the operation, but a fact is a fact,” Zelenskyy told journalists.
“We hit an Iskander launcher near our borders. I’m grateful to our soldiers who carry this out. This is our operation of hunting their systems that are positioned nearby,” he added.
The strike represents an important success precisely because Russian Iskander launchers are exceptionally difficult targets.
The Iskander is a road-mobile system capable of firing short-range ballistic missiles. Unlike fixed launch sites, its launchers can rapidly move into position, fire and leave before Ukrainian forces have time to locate and attack them.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said that mobility significantly complicates efforts to hunt the systems.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia generally positions the launchers more than 100 miles behind the front line, helping keep them beyond the reach of Ukrainian HIMARS strikes.
“Catching an Iskander on the move, or near the position where it’s deploying, is difficult,” he said.
Previously, reports emerged that Russia is maintaining a vast missile arsenal while its defense industry can produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles every month.
As of August 5, Russia had approximately 130 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M system allocated to its military grouping.
As of July, Moscow additionally possessed around 50 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles and approximately the same number of North Korean KN-23, KN-24, and KN-30 ballistic missiles.
