Moscow pulled out of the deal almost a year to the day later, alleging that Western sanctions continued to interfere with Russia’s own food and fertiliser exports. Despite this, both countries have largely continued to move their agricultural exports through the Black Sea – until now.
Nivievskyi said that the renewed blockade could prove far harsher than that of 2022.
“If you look at this from all angles, the situation is much worse,” he said. “The timing now is to plant winter crops, and winter crops are very important for Ukraine – winter wheat makes up the majority of the wheat that Ukraine produces.”
August is the height of Ukraine’s wheat harvest, and farmers would normally begin harvesting the country’s corn crop next month. If farmers can’t sell this year’s harvests, Nivievskyi said, many will struggle to raise the money they need to plant next year’s crops.
“For this, farmers they would need the liquidity, the working capital, to buy the seeds – and it’s not available right now,” he said. “Usually, around 50 percent of the harvest that’s sold in Ukraine is to purchase the materials for the autumn planting season, and this is now difficult to get because the prices are much lower, and volume-wise we cannot really sell as much as last season. And that’s going to be difficult.”
Storage pressures
With Ukraine’s grain exports down by some 75 percent year-on-year the first two weeks of August, the question of where exactly producers are going to store all the grain they can’t shift is becoming critical. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky said the country’s grain storage shortfall could reach as much as 11 million metric tonnes.
All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council deputy chairman Denys Marchuk told DW last week that Ukrainian farmers have already harvested more than 28 million tonnes of grains and pulses – and the corn harvest, estimated at some 33 million metric tonnes, hasn’t even begun.
“The capacities to store the exportable surpluses that Ukraine cannot really export right now are also limited -- and the major harvest is still in the fields,” Nivievskyi said. “So that's also going to create additional pressure on Ukrainian farmers, because they have to store the stuff somewhere.”
As local grain piles up, he added, domestic prices have only fallen further.
“Domestic prices in Ukraine now are quite low compared to the world market prices, and compared to the production costs,” he said. “There are messages and interviews of farmers saying that domestic prices are not at the level of production costs. So they will have to decide whether it’s worthwhile to bring the harvest in – or to keep it in the field.”
And while Russia is trying to reroute its grain shipments through the Caspian and Baltic Seas, Ukraine may struggle to find its own alternatives. The Danube River that has long served as Ukraine’s other major grain route has fallen to historically low levels as droughts wrack Europe, and the ports along its banks come under regular attack from Russian drones and missiles.
Nor can the country’s railways pick up the slack. Ukrainian authorities in July said Russia had damaged more than 200 locomotives in 2026 alone as Moscow systematically targets the country’s rolling stock. According to the agriculture minister, river and rails between them can carry just a third of what used to flow through Ukraine’s Black Sea ports.
Logistics aside, the political landscape has also changed considerably since the opening months of the full-scale war. Where the European Union once liberalised agricultural trade with the beleaguered country, suspending all import duties and quotas to help farmers move their produce west, the resulting influx of Ukrainian wheat and falling prices sparked fierce farmers’ protests across eastern and central Europe. Poland, Slovakia and Hungary all maintain bans on specific Ukrainian agricultural goods in the name of safeguarding their own farmers’ livelihoods.
"The willingness of European partners to help Ukraine out is also not there as it was in 2022," Nivievskyi said.

articles.title: Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
articles.body:
Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
TEHRAN- An open letter signed by a group of Western academics, writers, activists and former and current political prisoners has drawn criticism from other scholars and anti-war activists, who argue that its focus on Iran’s domestic developments risks obscuring the central issue of the conflict: the foreign military assault on the country.
The letter, addressed to what it calls Iran’s “prisoners of conscience,” condemns executions, arbitrary arrests, torture, alleged sham trials and the targeting of ethnic minorities. It describes Iranian political prisoners as being caught “between two blades of a scissors” — one representing the Islamic Republic and the other the United States and Israel.
The signatories call on the Iranian authorities to end executions and release political prisoners, while also calling on Washington and Israel to end what they describe as their “barbaric wars and brutal sanctions.”
The list of signatories includes figures such as Angela Davis, Mumia Abu-Jamal, Judith Butler, Rashid Khalidi, Robin D. G. Kelley, Ruth Wilson Gilmore and Walden Bello, among others.
 
 Yet the letter has prompted a broader debate over whether placing Iran’s political prisoners at the center of the discussion, while the country is under military attack, creates a misleading equivalence between domestic developments and an external war.
Critics question the letter’s political framing
One critic, writing under the name Carlos on X, described the letter as politically problematic despite believing that its signatories included people with long records of opposition to imperialism and political repression.
Noting the participation of figures including Davis, Abu-Jamal, Khalidi, Kelley, Gilmore and Butler, Carlos wrote that these were not people who could simply be dismissed; several had spent their lives in anti-imperialist and Black liberation movements.
But he argued that the letter nevertheless adopted 'a misleading framework.'
Its central metaphor, he wrote, was the image of the Islamic Republic on one side and US-Israeli imperialism on the other, with the Iranian people caught between them. According to Carlos, the framing “inserts a symmetry” between the two sides while failing to adequately distinguish between a state facing an external military attack and the domestic political system governing it.
Carlos also questioned the timing and potential political consequences of the letter. He argued that, regardless of what individual signatories intended, the text could function as part of a broader political narrative used to justify pressure on Iran.
He specifically criticized the letter for invoking allegations including sham trials, systematic torture and the targeting of minorities without providing detailed sourcing in the text. He argued that similar language has historically been used in campaigns preceding regime-change efforts.
His criticism was echoed, in a different form, by Ajamu Baraka, an international human-rights activist and political organizer. Baraka did not reject criticism of Iran itself. Instead, he distinguished between criticizing a government and taking a political position in the context of war.
“No one is above criticism,” Baraka wrote. “Comrades who signed that letter need to understand the difference between criticism & political positioning.”
He argued that the signatories had chosen a political position that, in his view, gave legitimacy to U.S. military violence against Iran.
The reaction from legal scholar Nina Farnia was also critical. Farnia shared material relating to the letter while defending her own position on the conflict. Her broader intervention questioned the decision by progressive voices in the United States and elsewhere to focus publicly on condemning Iran at a moment when, in her view, greater attention should be directed toward opposing the war and sanctions imposed by their own governments.
Historian and scholar Adnan A. Husain similarly questioned the political timing of the letter. In a post responding to the debate, he maintained that publishing an open letter focused on condemning Iran, while the United States and Israel were engaged in military and economic pressure against the country, risked shifting political attention away from opposition to the war.
Husain wrote that the Western left was moving toward public condemnation of Iran “just when” the United States was turning increasingly to economic pressure and political subversion. He argued that activists should instead organize against the war and sanctions imposed by their own government.
David Miller, Political sociologist, producer, and former professor at the University of Bristol said, all signed the disgraceful letter to the Guardian denouncing the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world’s leading anti-imperialist state.
Worse, they compare the Republic with the Zionist/US imperialist aggressor. What we (and they) should be doing is defending the Republic. The Islamic Republic of Iran is not only defending itself, the Palestinians, Lebanon, and the resistance movement. It’s also defending all of humanity and indeed civilization against the depredations of Jewish supremacist imperialism. This is an existential matter for the whole world.
Susan Abulhawa, Palestinian author and activist, has issued a sharp critique of mainstream framing that portrays the US-Israeli confrontation with Iran as a balanced conflict between two equal sides.
In a statement shared on her platform, Abulhawa argues that such framing ignores a "profound asymmetry of power." She describes Iran as a nation crippled by decades of sanctions, now fighting an "existential anti-imperial struggle," while facing a nuclear-armed U.S.-Israeli empire with unlimited military resources, surveillance, and near-total dominance over global political, legal, and information systems.
Abulhawa takes issue with minimizing language in a recent letter, which referred to "current, indiscriminate waves of US-Israeli military assaults." She says that this understates the scale of destruction, citing unprovoked attacks on a school that killed 180 children and teachers, the assassination of Iran's spiritual leader and much of its leadership, and strikes on civilian infrastructure including water systems, farmland, and power grids. She also highlights the downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the U.S., which killed 290 civilians, and decades of assassinations of Iranian scientists and commanders—all of which went unanswered.
The activist also criticizes the letter for failing to contextualize Iranian arrests of detainees, arguing that while some imprisonments may be wrongful, others involve individuals who confessed to espionage for Mossad or terrorism, including a group that brutally murdered a young Quran reciter. She insists that any fair assessment must engage with Iran's legitimate security concerns.
Abulhawa concludes that the conflict is not a symmetrical confrontation but an anti-imperial struggle against overwhelming imperial force distinction, she says, is crucial for honest analysis.
Questions over the signatories’ motives and the letter’s focus
Without direct statements from each signatory, it would be difficult to establish that they all interpreted the letter in precisely the same way.
The criticism therefore raises a legitimate journalistic question rather than providing a definitive answer: what exactly did each signatory intend to endorse?
That question is particularly relevant because the letter was published during a period of military confrontation. The document gives substantial attention to Iran’s domestic political developments, while the external conflict appears largely as one half of a broader framework of “dual oppression.”
For critics, this framing risks placing the government of a country under attack and the states conducting military operations against it within a single conceptual structure, without sufficiently addressing the different forms of power and responsibility involved.
But the timing and framing matter. A government’s policy inside the country and another state’s decision to wage war against that country are separate questions. They can both be condemned, but they carry different legal, political, and moral implications. Treating them as interchangeable risks obscuring the question of responsibility for the conflict itself.
The debate over the letter therefore goes beyond Iran’s domestic politics. It raises a broader question for international intellectual and human-rights circles: how should activists respond when a country facing external military attack is also accused of serious internal repression?
What remains less clear is whether all those whose names appear beneath the letter share the same interpretation of that argument.
That uncertainty is itself significant. The prominence of the signatories may lend the letter considerable political weight, but a list of names cannot, by itself, establish a uniform political position. Determining what each individual intended to endorse would require direct confirmation from the signatories themselves.
Its critics, however, contend that the document’s framing places the aggressor and the state under attack within an overly symmetrical narrative and risks diverting attention from the central question of the war: who initiated the military action, what legal basis was claimed for it, and who bears responsibility for its consequences?

articles.title: Nearly 100 pieces of Ukrainian military equipment on display in Kyiv at first-ever drone parade
articles.body:
Nearly 100 pieces of Ukrainian military equipment were showcased in Kyiv at the country's first-ever parade of air, land, and sea drones to mark Ukraine's Independence Day, specifically: 30 land-based robotic systems (LRS), nine unmanned boats, 18 air target interceptors, 27 bomber drones, eight reconnaissance drones, and seven drones designed for long-range strikes, according to the President's Office of Ukraine.
"Kyiv hosted the country's first-ever parade of air, ground, and maritime drones to mark Ukraine's Independence Day, featuring nearly 100 units of Ukrainian weaponry. And this is only a fraction of what our country can already be proud of," the office said on its website on Monday.
Earlier reports indicated that several dozen wheeled and tracked vehicles took part in the parade, which was not announced in advance and took place on the capital's main street at dawn on Independence Day without spectators.
As noted in the statement from the President's Office, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked everyone who helped Ukraine at the start of Russia's full-scale aggression, as well as those who continue to help now. He emphasized that the time has come for our country to help others with what makes this war unique and enables us to protect people's lives and our independence – unmanned technologies.
"This is what will allow Ukraine, after this war, to be a true provider of security for its partners – first and foremost for its friends, for our Europe, and for all those who have helped us. Ukraine knows how to be grateful. Ukraine knows how to be strong. But we have something to show. We have much to be grateful for to the Ukrainians who manufacture and deploy our weapons," the president said.
A video clip showed 30 ground-based robotic systems – designed to save the lives of Ukrainian soldiers – driving down Khreshchatyk Street: TerMIT, Lynx, Simba, Ardal, Zmiy, and Ratel.
The GRCs conduct reconnaissance, lay and clear mines, deliver ammunition, provisions, and equipment, and evacuate the wounded. They also provide fire support and assist in storming enemy positions. Ground robotic systems are capable of carrying loads weighing up to 600 kilograms and traveling dozens of kilometers. This year alone, GRCs have carried out more than 66,000 missions. In 2026, the Defense Forces contracted for more than 22,000 domestically produced ground-based robotic systems.
A fleet of nine Ukrainian unmanned boats, developed during the war and tested in combat conditions, sailed down the Dnipro River. "It was these vessels that deprived the enemy of its dominance in the Black Sea and forced a significant portion of the Russian fleet to leave the temporarily occupied Crimea," the statement reads.
The multi-purpose combat platforms Sea Baby, Mahura, and Sarhan carry out missions involving reconnaissance, patrolling, strikes against maritime targets, and the launch of our drones. Ukrainian bombers are capable of carrying tens of kilograms of payload and operating at ranges of tens of kilometers.

The SHARK can remain airborne for up to seven hours and cover a distance of up to 420 kilometers. The LF-400 not only conducts surveillance but also carries strike drones, delivering them closer to the combat mission area.

It is these drones that carry out Ukraine's precision strikes, traveling hundreds and thousands of kilometers from the front lines to strike the very things that fuel the Russian war machine: military factories, ammunition and fuel depots, logistics hubs, airfields, and other military facilities. Last year alone, these drones carried out nearly 2,000 strikes and hit over 1,000 confirmed targets on enemy territory.

articles.title: To further isolate Iran's economy, U.S. rolls out 'D-Day' sanctions
articles.body:
To further isolate Iran’s economy, U.S. rolls out ‘D-Day’ sanctions
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Iranian officials downplayed the significance of the pressure campaign, and suggested it could shut down all oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
- Bessent’s plan to potentially squeeze major economies like China and India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk to the U.S.
WASHINGTON — The United States unveiled plans Monday for new sanctions against Iran that Trump administration officials said are designed to sever Tehran from the global financial system as the nearly six-month conflict between the two countries drags on.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who previewed the announcement last week as “economic D-Day,” described the measures as the opening of an all-out financial assault on the Iranian government and its trade partners — a group that includes China, India, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates.
“To those who enable Tehran, do not discount the cost of testing Washington’s resolve,” Bessent said at a news conference. “No nation should expect to enjoy the rewards of our system while helping those who seek to destroy it.”
Bessent said it was time for world leaders to “make a decision” between “America and Iran,” adding that President Trump has already been calling foreign leaders to make specific requests ahead of the new sanctions.
But when asked whom the president had been talking to, Bessent said he would not “name names.” He also said the secondary measure would not take effect immediately, arguing that the administration is trying to give “everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior.”
“Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent said when a reporter pressed him on why the sanctions weren’t immediate. “We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly and that we are serious.”
After trade negotiations collapsed, President Trump’s 50% tariffs on scores of Canadian imports kicked in over the weekend. A look at what that means.
The pressure campaign will build on a naval blockade and other sanctions the Trump administration has already imposed in its effort to force Tehran into a deal that ends the war on U.S. terms.
Trump’s latest economic push against Iran revives a familiar strategy from presidents of both parties, using financial leverage to pressure Tehran toward more serious negotiations over its nuclear program. Sanctions helped bring Iran to the table before a 2015 nuclear deal brokered by President Obama, but the agreement was widely criticized as weak by Republicans. After Trump withdrew from the agreement in his first term, a new “maximum pressure” campaign failed to secure a new deal.
Trump’s decision to return to a strategy of economic coercion has signaled to Iran that the fighting phase of the war is probably over, for now, with the U.S. administration choosing a path “neither of war nor of peace,” Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, said this week.
Iranian officials, who had been anticipating the move, pushed back on Washington’s strategy even before Bessent began speaking Monday.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian state media over the weekend that the sanctions amounted to a repackaged version of decades-old American pressure tactics that Tehran has already learned to withstand. Esmail Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman, warned of “grave consequences” for any countries cooperating with what he said was “illegal behavior” by the United States. And Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme Security Council, suggested that the economic pressure could shut down oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, a threat that would ripple through global energy markets.
That defiance underscores the central gamble of Washington’s strategy. Rather than aiming sanctions at Iran alone, Bessent’s plan to potentially squeeze major economies like China and India over their ties to Tehran could pose a diplomatic risk to the U.S.
The fallout could also reach beyond foreign diplomacy as a hit to global markets also risks compounding Trump’s troubles at home ahead of the midterm elections, as Americans grow unhappy with the economy and their support for the conflict in the Middle East plummets. The Iran sanctions also land as the administration wages a separate trade fight with Canada, adding uncertainty to global and domestic markets.
Whether Washington will be able to apply pressure on Iran’s trade partners remains an open question.
China alone shares nearly $10 billion in bilateral trade with Iran, and paid roughly $31.2 billion for unreported Iranian crude oil imports in 2025, according to the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. That makes China the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil by a wide margin, accounting for more than 90% of Iran’s oil exports, according to the commission.
It is unclear whether Trump has spoken to China’s leader, Xi Jinping, about the sanctions. But the two leaders are set to meet in Washington next month, adding to the diplomatic dynamics of the moment.
Other trading partners have already made some moves.
The UAE said last week that it was suspending trade with Iran, a decision that followed accusations that Tehran had fired two ballistic missiles at the Emirates.
Afra Al Hameli, a spokesperson for the Emirati Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a post on Aug. 18 on X that all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice. She added that the Emirates was “firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system.”
Bessent said Monday that he expects other countries will “take similar actions as we continue our engagement.”
In an opinion article written for the Financial Times last week, Bessent has cast the new measures as the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary.”
Bessent wrote that countries that “sever Iran’s remaining financial and commercial connectivity” will see their economies reinvigorated, and those who don’t will experience the end of their “lasting prosperity.”
President Trump is betting ramped-up economic pressure against Iran’s trading partners can finally force Tehran to accept a peace deal on U.S. terms. But, as with similar efforts before, Iran may be impervious to such pressure.
“Any nation that serves as a financial artery of a withering regime should expect to share in its isolation,” he wrote. “To become a sanctuary for terror is to become, in the eyes of the United States, a global pariah.”
Ahead of the announcement Monday, Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran was “completely collapsing.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said the U.S. had already done all that it can against Iran and that the central bank had been shoring up its foreign currency reserves for months. Last week, he said Iran’s crude exports had “virtually stopped.”
“[The Americans] have done everything, so what else can they do?” he said in an interview with Tasnim News.
Despite his assurances that the central bank was working on preventing a devaluation of the Iranian rial, the currency has struggled to remain above a black market exchange rate of 2 million per dollar — a record low. The Central Bank rate stands at roughly 1.5 million rial to the dollar.
Though experts question the effectiveness of additional economic pressure on Tehran, Bessent’s threat to target Iran’s trading partners — especially the UAE, China and Turkey, who together comprise almost three-quarters of Iran’s foreign imports — will undoubtedly be painful for Iranians.
For example, Iran uses the UAE as a reexport hub and buffer, and receives vehicle spare parts from China, according to the Observatory for Economic Complexity. Iranian economic experts say both the agricultural and pharmaceutical sectors also rely on imports from countries such as Brazil and Turkey.
Ceballos reported from Washington and Bulos from Beirut.

It is about €340 billion, whereas in 2027 we will spend €140 billion. So we need to be competitive in the number of long-range strikes,” the president said.
He explained that he was referring not to ballistic missiles but to other strike capabilities.

Leaders of the Coalition of the Willing have said after their meeting in Kyiv that they have agreed to step up military support for Ukraine, boost its air defence capabilities, impose further sanctions on Russia and prepare multinational forces.
Source: a joint statement by the leaders of the Coalition of the Willing posted on the UK government website, as reported by European Pravda

"They expressed their determination to increase military support to Ukraine, strengthen its air defence as a matter of urgent priority, enhance cooperation with its defence industry, and share relevant technologies, including through the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition," the statement said.
They also agreed to step up sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex and those supporting its operations, to provide immediate energy support for Ukraine to prepare for the coming winter. They stressed the need to support Ukraine's economic resilience amid Russia's attempts to block exports through Black Sea ports.
The leaders agreed to continue efforts to restrict Russia's financial resources for waging the war through sanctions and measures to combat sanctions circumvention, including action against Russia's shadow fleet.

articles.title: General Atomics Plans ‘Wildfire’ Drone for Pentagon’s Low-Cost MMA Program
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems predicts the new drone it plans to pitch for the military’s “Massed Modular Aircraft” program will exceed many of the military’s requirements for a successor to the MQ-9 Reaper.
Wildfire, as General Atomics has dubbed it, “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” company spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement, though he declined to specify the drone’s expected capabilities or cost. Aviation Week first reported the company’s plans for Wildfire.
MMA is intended to be a low-cost, attritable drone that could fly in groups if needed and take on some missions now performed by the MQ-9 Reaper, which was also made by General Atomics. The Defense Innovation Unit released a solicitation July 7 asking companies to submit ideas for the new drone concept, which is meant “to execute missions that the MQ-9A performs today.”
The Air Force is partnering with DIU on the MMA effort, which it said “will directly inform the requirements for the MQ-9’s successor.”
DIU’s solicitation called for drones to be able to carry a payload of at least 2,800 pounds—roughly the weight of one Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile, or LRASM—and have an unrefueled combat radius of at least 2,300 nautical miles, while carrying a payload, as well as being able to fly a one-way ferrying flight of at least 8,000 nautical miles.
The Pentagon wants MMA drones to be able to launch weapons, collect intelligence, conduct electronic warfare, or relay communications while staying airborne for long periods. DIU said that is intended to exhaust an enemy and force them to burn through pricey anti-aircraft missiles and other resources.
While General Atomics did not detail what Wildfire—a medium-altitude long endurance drone—will be able to do, Brinkley’s statement hinted at some of the goals the company set out to achieve.
“How do we come out of the box, day one, with a 10,000 nautical mile ferry range?” Brinkley said. “Can we carry four LRASMs? Can we swarm 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control? Can we fuse all of that data into a highly effective common operating picture? Can we do that at scalable, affordable mass?”
The Air Force has lost dozens of MQ-9 drones since operations against Iran launched in late February. The Washington Post reported earlier in August that about 45 Reapers have been lost, in some cases shot down, during Operation Epic Fury.
In its original solicitation, DIU said that with adversaries increasingly using low-cost antiaircraft capabilities to create layered defenses, the military won’t be able to rely on “exquisite” aircraft with price tags north of $30 million. For that reason, DIU and the Air Force said, the military needs drone capabilities that can weather some losses while still being able to accomplish their missions.
The Air Force and DIU want these new drones to be modular so they can be quickly updated with payloads like full-motion video sensors, so an MMA could carry out some of the MQ-9’s current missions. An Air Force official told reporters earlier in August that the service wants to start awarding contracts by the end of this year.
DIU also wants contractors to be able to flight test a full-scale prototype 21 months after receiving the award and to be able to deliver 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031.
Brinkley said General Atomics “can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”
However, Brinkley said, the military has an “immediate, critical ISR gap” that Wildfire would not be able to fill in the short term. General Atomics has options that could serve as an interim bridge, he said, and the company is now discussing those with Pentagon decision-makers.
General Atomics did not reveal any imagery or concept art for Wildfire.

articles.title: Ukraine’s robot and drone parade offers a glimpse of the future of war
articles.body:
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day with a military display unlike any it had staged before: robots on the streets of Kyiv, naval drones on the Dnipro river and UAVs in the skies above the capital, showcasing technologies that have transformed the battlefield since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
There were no marching soldiers, no tanks and no columns of heavy armour. In their place came robots designed to perform many of the same tasks.
Marking 35 years of independence, Ukraine staged a different kind of military parade on Monday, showcasing its defence technology and unmanned warfare capabilities.
The parade offered a glimpse of the future of warfare and how profoundly four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion have transformed the Ukrainian military.
Dozens of multi-role unmanned ground vehicles moved along Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s main street, including robotic systems designed for combat, reconnaissance, logistics and the evacuation of wounded soldiers from the battlefield.
On the Dnipro river, Ukraine displayed the naval drones that have helped it challenge Russia’s once-dominant Black Sea Fleet despite possessing no conventional fleet of comparable size.
They included variants of the Magura and Sea Baby families of unmanned vessels, which Ukraine has used to strike Russian warships, military infrastructure and other targets.
Above the capital flew another generation of machines that has become indispensable on Ukraine’s battlefields: reconnaissance and strike UAVs, alongside interceptor drones developed to shoot down Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities around the clock.
The parade offered a snapshot of a military transformation that has taken place at extraordinary speed and scale since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Four and a half years later unmanned systems have become central to operations across land, sea and air, performing tasks once entrusted overwhelmingly to soldiers, aircraft, ships and armoured vehicles.
In 2024, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed legislation creating the Unmanned Systems Forces — a separate branch of the military dedicated to drone warfare — making Ukraine the first country to establish an independent branch built around unmanned systems.
The innovation reflects both technological development and brutal necessity.
Ukraine is defending itself against a much larger country with greater reserves of soldiers and conventional weapons.
Unmanned systems have allowed Kyiv to strike Russian forces while reducing the exposure of its own troops, especially infantry, extend the reach of relatively inexpensive weapons, and compensate for shortages ranging from artillery ammunition to naval power.
Monday’s display brought those strands of the war together in the centre of Kyiv.
Ukraine has not held a conventional military parade since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.
In previous years, Khreshchatyk became better known for a very different display of military hardware: burnt-down Russian tanks and armoured vehicles captured or destroyed on the battlefield.

articles.title: Ukraine, UK sign landmark AI deal
articles.body:
Ukraine, UK sign landmark AI deal
Ukrinform reports this with reference to the UK government.
The AI partnership agreement, signed in Kyiv by President Volodymyr Zelensky and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, will give Ukraine access to support from world-leading universities, researchers and technology companies, as well as the world's third-largest AI ecosystem.
The UK is set to become the first international partner to gain access to Ukraine's Avengers AI Labs, enabling the two countries to accelerate the development of AI tools designed to shape the battlefield.
“By combining Ukrainian battlefield data with British expertise, we will accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home,” the UK government said.
The platform provides real world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine.
These sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, including tanks, artillery, air defense systems, infantry and aerial targets such as Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, feeding the data into Avengers AI Labs to train new AI models.
Under the partnership, the UK and Ukraine will also explore other platforms for cooperation.
The UK government described Avengers AI Labs as “a goldmine of battlefield data” that will give British innovators and researchers unprecedented access to real operational data and the ability to rapidly develop and test new technologies.
In turn, the UK will provide Ukraine with access to world-leading universities, researchers, technology companies and its extensive AI ecosystem, enabling Ukraine to draw on British expertise to accelerate the development of solutions to urgent challenges and turn hard-won battlefield experience and unique datasets into technologies that will benefit both countries.
“This groundbreaking partnership will bring together Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience with Britain’s world-class AI ecosystem, giving us the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine,” Prime Minister Burnham said.
“Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading innovators in defence technology, forged through courage, ingenuity and the hard lessons of war,” he added.
As reported, during his first foreign trip as Prime Minister, Burnham assured Ukraine that he would work to strengthen assistance to the country, particularly in air defense and countering Russian missile strikes.
Earlier, the UK government announced that it would allow European defense company MBDA to declassify information on British components used in Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles for Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
Ukrainian drones reached Russia’s northern Arkhangelsk region, home to the strategic Plesetsk military cosmodrome used to launch military satellites and intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to OSINT analysis published by Russian independent media outlet Astra on August 23.
The incident appears to mark the first documented case of Ukrainian drones reaching the Arkhangelsk region, extending Kyiv’s deep-strike reach into Russia’s far north.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian monitoring resource Locator Rossii reported that at least two drones reached the Plesetsk area.
ASTRA analyzed photographs taken by local residents and said smoke could be seen rising in the vicinity of the military spaceport. The images were reportedly taken from Mirny, a closed city established during the Soviet era specifically to support operations at Plesetsk.
The exact target and consequences of the reported drone operation remain unclear.
Astra also geolocated footage published by Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ showing a drone flying above Kargopol in the Arkhangelsk region. The aircraft was traveling in the direction of Plesetsk, located roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, away.
Local residents separately recorded two drones flying through the region and posted footage of the aircraft online.
Temporary flight restrictions were introduced at an airfield near the Plesetsk Cosmodrome because of the potential drone threat, under Russia’s emergency airspace closure procedure known as the Carpet Plan.
Plesetsk is Russia’s principal northern military spaceport and plays a significant role in both its military space program and strategic missile testing.
Russia has repeatedly launched Soyuz-2 and Angara rockets carrying military spacecraft from the facility. The cosmodrome is also being used to deploy Rassvet communications satellites, part of Moscow’s effort to build a domestic satellite internet network comparable to SpaceX’s Starlink.
Russia plans to have 292 Rassvet communications satellites in orbit by the end of 2027, making the program increasingly important for Moscow’s communications infrastructure.
Plesetsk also serves a separate strategic military role as a launch site for Russian intercontinental ballistic missiles.
No confirmed information has yet emerged regarding damage at the cosmodrome or whether Plesetsk was the drones’ intended target.
Russia continues to deploy its “Rassvet” satellite constellation, which is intended to serve as an analogue to Starlink.
However, the project requires regular launches of carrier rockets. The first two groups of Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit using Soyuz-2.1b rockets manufactured by the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara.
Production of carrier rockets is one of the key constraints on the deployment of the constellation. The satellites can also be launched from the Plesetsk and Vostochny spaceports in Russia, as well as the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: 'It's war against the West' — Latvian PM on Russian provocations against European countries
articles.body:
'It's war against the West' — Latvian PM on Russian provocations against European countries
Russia poses a growing hybrid threat to Europe, using disinformation, migration, and other tactics to destabilize the continent, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said on Aug. 24 during a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv.
"That's the war of Russia against the West, the EU, and NATO, as we've seen," Kulbergs said.
Russia has long used hybrid warfare tactics across Europe including sabotage cyberattacks, disinformation. Cases of each have escalated since the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with several drone incursions recorded in recent years.
Kulbergs said the EU was also seeing attacks on its border, highlighting how Russia is using Belarus to organize a migration crisis toward the bloc.
"We see that it is one of the highest threats, with a case that is well organized by the Kremlin through the hands of Belarus and through criminal organizations that are also making money from it as a service," Kulbergs said.
"This is testing our ability to fight back, our technical ability, our reaction times," he added.
Belarus has previously been accused by European countries of deliberately facilitating irregular migration to the EU's eastern borders as a form of hybrid warfare. Minsk helped channel migrants from the Middle East, Africa, and Asia toward Lithuania, Latvia and Poland after the EU imposed sanctions on Belarus in 2021. The Kremlin has also been accused of supporting the renewed campaign.
Kulbergs said migration was only one part of a broader campaign that also includes cyberattacks and attempts to disrupt elections and influence public opinion.
"We also see cyberattacks happening. We see potential disruptions of public aspects, as we've seen in many countries — attacking elections, trying to disrupt the mindset of the people," he said.
The Baltic states have faced a series of drone incidents in recent months. In May, Lithuania issued its first air raid alert over a suspected drone threat after an unidentified drone crossed into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. Fighter jets operating as part of NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace on Aug. 14, according to the Latvian military.
More recently, Lithuania said on Aug. 6 that it had intelligence suggesting Russia could use Ukrainian-made drones in false-flag attacks against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robert Kaunas said Russia was considering "unconventional kinetic attacks" as tensions rose following repeated drone incursions across the region.
Kulbergs said Russia's actions had ultimately strengthened NATO rather than weakening it.
"Russia does not understand. They have actually made us stronger together. They have made NATO stronger. We now have Sweden and Finland joining in," he said.

articles.title: Bessent warns countries defying US sanctions will 'share in isolation' of Iran
articles.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that any country that continues to enable Iran will become part of US efforts to "isolate" Tehran from the global economy, adding that US President Donald Trump is already calling on world leaders to halt trade with Iran.
Bessent unveiled new sanctions on Iran on Monday — targeting Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping — escalating the Trump administration’s pressure on Tehran to negotiate a deal to end the conflict and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
"Iran's enablers purchase, transport its petroleum. They facilitate the flow of its finances through exchange houses and free trade zones. They welcome Iran's flights and maintain registries on its behalf. They turn a blind eye to seaborne fuel transfers and overland transits. They condone illicit use of their banks, all the while concealing the extent of their complicity," Bessent told media in Washington DC, without naming the countries.
He said every country has a defined timeline to shut down activities the US has identified, warning, "If they do not take action, we will do so unilaterally through Treasury authorities."
He said President Trump is making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with Iran.
"We are already seeing results over the weekend," he added.
View on China
Bessent said that countries and entities that stand with the US "will reap the rewards of our partnership", but warned "those who tether themselves to the Iranian regime should expect to share in the isolation of a withering regime."
He stated that delegations from the US Treasury, State Department, and military are engaging international counterparts to urge decisive action.
Bessent said that Washington would end access to the US dollar system for those laundering Iranian money, as he sought to ramp up pressure targeting Tehran months into war.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking."
Analysts say the impact of Bessent's announcement hinges on whether Iran's key trading partners, such as China, view US warnings as credible.
Asked if Chinese banks dealing with Iran could be targeted, Bessent said "no one is above the reach of US sanctions."
"An economic engagement of any kind with this murderous regime will expose those responsible to the full reach of American power."
The US has long sanctioned Iran, though Tehran has frequently bypassed these restrictions through front companies.
Iran rejects Bessent's 'bombast'
While Bessent was speaking in Washington, the speaker of the Iranian Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, took to X, saying: "Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries."
"Iran's trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don't take these statements into account anywhere."
US joined Israel in attacking Iran on February 28, with strikes quickly killing the longtime supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and much of the other top brass as well as hundreds of civilians.
But Iran quickly hit back by exerting control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passageway through which one-fifth of global oil once sailed, and it has rained missiles and drones on US-allied Gulf Arab monarchies, shattering the oil-rich countries' hard-earned reputation for stability.
Tehran has reported thousands of Iranian fatalities as it struck US bases and assets in the Middle East, while the Pentagon has confirmed 18 deaths in addition to 756 injuries among its personnel during the conflict.

articles.title: Houthis claim strike on Saudi tanker in latest Red Sea escalation
articles.body:
The missile struck a tanker 63 nautical miles west of Yanbu, setting it ablaze, in the latest strike under the Houthis' announced blockade of Saudi Arabia, threatening its ability to export millions of barrels of crude oil per day.
Yemen's Houthis said on Monday that their forces hit a Saudi oil tanker in the Red Sea with a ballistic missile, as the Iran-backed group continues to pursue a maritime blockade of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another crucial artery for global shipping.
"The strike was accurate and direct, resulting in a fire breaking out aboard the vessel and causing a number of other ships that were present in the target area to flee," the Houthis said in a statement.
"This targeting comes as part of the implementation of the Armed Forces' decision to ban maritime navigation by the Saudi enemy."
The Houthi claim came hours after a British maritime agency said a tanker struck by an "unknown projectile" caught fire off Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.
"The Company Security Officer reported a tanker has been struck by (an) unknown projectile causing a fire to the vessel on the main deck," said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.
"All crew are safe and accounted for and no environmental impact has been reported," it added.
The incident took place 63 nautical miles west of the Saudi city of Yanbu, the agency reported. Yanbu lies hundreds of kilometres north of Yemen.
British maritime security firm Vanguard Tech also said a Saudi-flagged vessel had been hit by a missile and caught fire.
The Bab al-Mandeb strait, which connects the southern Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, carries roughly 12% of global maritime trade.
The Houthis disrupted it severely with their campaign against Israel-linked shipping during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, claiming it was in a show of support for Palestinians.
The Bab el-Mandeb campaign comes at a time when the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf's other critical chokepoint, remains under blockade after the US-Iran war continued following the collapse of the interim deal between the two sides.
The Houthis have reportedly held talks with Tehran on instituting a toll for cargo ships passing through the strait akin to the one Iran is eyeing for Hormuz.
Turning up the heat
The group — formally known as Ansar Allah — has been attacking Saudi Arabia's ships after declaring a maritime blockade of the country last month.
Hostilities erupted in July after the group welcomed an Iranian plane in Yemen's capital Sana'a, setting off a spate of tit-for-tat attacks.
The Houthis have hit Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and attacked Yemeni government forces since the latest round of fighting broke out.
They have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and airports.
Riyadh has since launched air strikes on Houthi military positions and infrastructure in Hodeidah, Yemen's main Red Sea port.
The blockade has threatened Saudi Arabia's ability to export millions of barrels of crude oil per day.
On 31 July, Riyadh announced a new multinational maritime defence coalition, with 14 countries, including Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, signing a founding statement to protect Red Sea shipping.
Embroiled in more than a decade of its own war, Yemen became the latest country to be dragged into the Iran war last month, when the Houthis upended a 2022 truce with the country's internationally recognised government.
The Houthis, who came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile, are part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance.
The Axis is a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, which are all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.
While the Houthis do not control the part of Yemen’s coastline along Bab el-Mandeb, they hold territory less than 100 kilometres away.

articles.title: Zelensky: There Is No Doubt – Ukraine Will Always Be Independent
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky marked the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence on Monday, Aug. 24, declaring the country will “always” remain sovereign.
The Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine was adopted by parliament in 1991, following the failed Soviet coup – also known as the “August Coup.” During the short-lived attempt to seize power, Communist Party officials placed then-President Mikhail Gorbachev under house arrest.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“There is no doubt about it,” Zelensky said in a statement. “Ukrainians will not submit to what they do not believe in, and they certainly will not abandon their dream – the dream of living, the dream of living independently.”
Rejecting submission
Zelensky used the anniversary to reject framing Ukraine’s sovereignty as a matter of negotiation between larger powers.
“Ukrainians will not be paving stones beneath the feet of tsars and leaders,” he said, adding that Ukrainians will not be “a bargaining chip in disputes between capitals” either.
State awards given to soldiers and civilians
In a separate statement posted to his Telegram shortly afterward, Zelensky said the anniversary was also marked with state honors for those who have sustained Ukraine’s existence through the war.
“In honor of our greatest national holiday, we are presenting Ukrainian state awards to those without whom Ukraine would not exist, ” he said, honoring soldiers and fallen civilians posthumously.
He also awarded battle flags and ribbons of the distinction “For Courage and Valor” to military units.
Ukraine at 35: The Nation Dudayev Warned Russia Could Not Subdue
Among those honored posthumously, Zelensky named Junior Lieutenant Nazariy Hryntsevych (call sign “Grenka”), head of the search organization “Platsdarm” Oleksii Yukov, and schoolboy Stepan Chubenko – who was killed by Russian militants.
Recognition for public figures
Several prominent Ukrainians were also recognized for their contributions, including sport shooting champion Olena Kostevych, Superhumans rehabilitation center director Olha Rudnieva, Bishop Vitali Kryvytski, and artist Anatoliy Kryvolap and singer Zlata Ohnevich.
“I want to thank every person who makes their personal contribution to ensuring that Ukraine not merely preserves but consistently strengthens its independence,” Zelensky said.
“Thank you for being part of Ukraine, and for our state being able to be proud of you,” he continued.
His remarks came as 10 Ukrainian servicemen, who had been listed as missing in action, returned home via Belarus earlier that day.
In addition, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv on Monday for his first official visit to Ukraine as the country celebrated its independence, while the UK government agreed to permit defense company MBDA to declassify information on British components used in Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles.
The decision follows the UK’s 2023 delivery of long-range weapons to Ukraine.

articles.title: NYT: A fully autonomous Russian AI drone run by an Nvidia minicomputer killed 3 civilians in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia
articles.body:
NYT: A fully autonomous Russian AI drone run by an Nvidia minicomputer killed 3 civilians in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia
A Russian drone guided entirely by an experimental artificial intelligence system killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia, according to an article in The New York Times (NYT).
Russian drones attacked a gas station on July 6, killing a 19-year-old university student and two men, ages 41 and 48.
The NYT’s account rests on the findings of Ukrainian drone experts, military officials, and forensic investigators who examined the wreckage of that drone and of other Russian Molniya drones that struck Zaporizhzhia. Here’s why they believe the drones were fully autonomous:
- The drones had no antennas for communicating with an operator, though they did carry video cameras.
- The drone that exploded and killed the three was flying in a group of about six. None of them was transmitting radio signals.
- The drones were launched at Zaporizhzhia in waves, with one large-scale attack following another.
- Inside the drones, investigators found Nvidia Jetson Orin minicomputers. Nvidia makes a large share of the chips that power the world’s most advanced AI systems. The minicomputers, which cost only a few hundred dollars, are believed to be what made the targeting decisions. Similar minicomputers have turned up in other Russian weapons.
- Ukrainian officials said the Nvidia minicomputer in the drone that struck Zaporizhzhia was not encrypted, allowing experts to view the terrain images loaded into the module. The drone could use those images to stay on its programmed course. The experts also examined the drone’s code, which, they said, showed what kinds of targets it had been trained to recognize and attack.
The drones are believed to work like this: an operator programs a drone to fly toward a specific target, such as a gas station; as it approaches, the drone picks its final target — propane tanks, for instance — on its own, drawing on prior training to recognize such containers.
Ukrainian officials said some of the Russian AI-equipped drones exploded during the attack, while others failed to detonate and stayed largely intact. They showed NYT reporters the wreckage of two such drones, and the reporters photographed the Nvidia module inside each. The wreckage of the drone that killed the three civilians does not appear in the NYT article. Ukraine had found similar wreckage — no antenna, but a camera and a minicomputer — even before the July 6 attack.
Both Russia and Ukraine are experimenting with AI in several drone models. Until now, machine vision has been used at scale only in the final stage of an attack, locking onto a target automatically after an operator has already chosen it. Fully autonomous AI is meant to remove the human from that final targeting decision.
Ukraine said Russia has been testing autonomous AI drones in Zaporizhzhia since May. In Russian-annexed Crimea, Ukraine’s armed forces are conducting their own tests of AI systems that select targets independently, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said. No deaths from those attacks have been reported so far.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: 2 children among 4 killed in Gaza a week after US asked Israel to curb attacks
articles.body:
2 children among 4 killed in Gaza a week after US asked Israel to curb attacks
DEIR AL-BALAH, Gaza Strip (AP) — Palestinian residents of war-battered Gaza fled homes and businesses as Israeli strikes and tank fire killed at least four people Monday, including two children, hospital officials said, a week after a U.S. delegation asked Israel to draw down attacks.
After evacuation warnings by Israel’s military, a strike hit a building in the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza. One family was unable to flee and a 4-year-old child was killed, according to Awda Hospital, where he was taken. His mother and sister were wounded. There was no Israeli military comment.
Israeli strikes hit three other buildings across the territory after residents said they received evacuation warnings. Some people sprinted away, with mothers carrying children, while others moved amid the rubble in wheelchairs or with canes.
Smoke rose over the already devastated landscape.
Israel’s military said it carried out strikes in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City and in Deir al-Balah after issuing warnings, targeting what it described as two Hamas weapons storage facilities inside mosques. The military did not provide evidence but said the facilities contained dozens of “Kalashnikov rifles, magazines and additional military equipment.”
An earlier Israeli strike on a tent in Deir al-Balah killed a man, according to Al-Aqsa Hospital, where his body was taken. Israel’s military said it killed a militant affiliated with Hamas’ special forces unit.
Others were killed or hurt in Khan Younis in the south
A man was killed and five others were wounded in an Israeli strike in Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Nasser Hospital, which received the casualties.
And Israeli tank fire hit an area east of Khan Younis, killing a 10-year-old girl, according to the hospital, where her body was taken.
Israel’s military did not immediately comment on the strike in Khan Younis and said it was not aware of the incident with the child.
Israel has continued to carry out targeted killings in the week since a U.S. delegation met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an effort to push last year’s ceasefire deal forward.
U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner asked Netanyahu to draw down Israel’s attacks in Gaza, a person familiar with the meeting said last week, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief journalists.
Israel has announced strikes on six of the seven days since that meeting.
Israel says it is targeting militants and related sites
While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the ceasefire took hold in October, Israeli airstrikes have killed at least 1,288 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains detailed casualty records that are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Militants have carried out shooting attacks on Israeli troops, and Israel says its strikes are in response to that and other ceasefire violations. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire.
Palestinian officials have reported strikes on homes and police stations, and Hamas has claimed that attacks are designed to destabilize Gaza and prevent progress on the ceasefire’s next steps, which include demilitarizing and reconstructing the territory and the deployment of an international stabilization force.
Israel warns against kites sent from Gaza
In the period before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel that sparked the war, burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into Israel, causing fires and other damage.
Now Israeli officials are expressing concern after several kites were found in a kibbutz near Gaza. No weapons or dangerous materials were attached. Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz in a statement Sunday threatened to ramp up strikes on Gaza unless Hamas ensures the kites stop flying toward Israel.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem has called the kites “essentially children’s toys” and accused Israel of using them as “an attempt to justify the continuation of aggression and violations against our people.”
The Oct. 7 attack killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. All hostages or their remains were later released. Israel’s retaliatory offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,422 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
___
AlJoud reported from Beirut. AP writer Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

articles.title: US unveils ‘economic onslaught’ against Iran
articles.body:
US unveils ‘economic onslaught’ against Iran
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has announced new sanctions against Iran, and threatened to boot any country dealing financially with Tehran out of the US dollar system, in a bid to make Iran an “economic outcast.”
The new sanctions target nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that allegedly trade in “illicit nuclear and missile technology” with Iran, aid Iran’s “cyber operations,” and move Iranian oil, the US Treasury Department said in a statement on Monday. More than a third of the sanctioned entities and individuals – 21 – are based in China.
The Treasury also said it had identified digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping as areas for potential secondary sanctions.
Speaking at a press conference later on Monday, Bessent went further, announcing the beginning of “Operation Economic Outcast,” which he described as “an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe.”
In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections… pic.twitter.com/1fLyobUucu
— Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (@SecScottBessent) August 24, 2026
Bessent explained that the US would penalize any country refusing to sever its economic ties with Tehran. “Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system,” he said, adding “the clock just started ticking.”
Iran exports goods to 147 countries, and imports from 114, according to the most recent data from the World Bank. Asked how the US intends to force three quarters of the world’s nations to cease trade with Iran, Bessent said that US President Donald Trump phoned multiple world leaders over the weekend “with specific requests to cease their interactions” with Iran, and that every country had been given “a defined timeline” to comply with his demands.
Bessent refused to share any more details, telling reporters that “we’re not going to name names,” nor was he “going to set timelines.” Pressed on whether Washington expected China – which is Iran’s largest trading partner – to abide by the sanctions regime, Bessent did not give a definitive answer.
“We find that the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy. And we are level-setting with every country to tell them our expectations. We know who they are. They know who they are,” he replied, adding “no-one is above the reach of US sanctions.”
Bessent’s threats were shrugged off in Tehran. “Americans know that no one buys their bombast,” senior Iranian negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X after the treasury secretary's press conference.
“The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries,”he explained. “Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere.”
Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned on Sunday that “not a single drop of oil will leave the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz” if the Gulf states join the US’ economic pressure campaign. If US President Donald Trump “wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Rezaei added.
Last week, Trump threatened to inflict what he called “Economic D-Day” on Iran, after a 60-day window for negotiating peace with Tehran expired with no breakthrough. Trump ruled out a return to negotiations, but Pakistani Chief of Defense Forces Asim Munir arrived in Tehran on Monday in an attempt to revive the talks.

articles.title: Neighbor accuses Sudan of cross-border airstrikes
articles.body:
Neighbor accuses Sudan of cross-border airstrikes
Chad has accused parties in Sudan’s civil war of carrying out airstrikes deep inside its territory, warning that the conflict risks spilling across the border, the Chadian Armed Forces said on Saturday.
According to the statement, aircraft and drones believed to belong to the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) or forces supporting them pursued and bombed a convoy of vehicles on Thursday. The strikes began on Sudanese soil before continuing more than 100 kilometers inside Chad, reaching the Mourdi department in the eastern Ennedi-Est province.
The military said that the extent of the incursion was established following aerial and ground checks conducted on Friday. No Chadian casualties have been reported, but the army condemned what it described as a new violation of the country’s territorial integrity.
Chad warned Sudan’s warring parties against attempting to extend the conflict onto its territory, saying that its defense and security forces remain on the highest level of alert and are prepared to respond to any threat to the country’s security. There has been no response from Sudanese authorities to the Chadian military’s allegations.
Sudan plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The incident follows several previous cases of violence spilling across the Sudan-Chad border. In July, a drone arriving from Sudanese territory struck the eastern Chadian border town of Tine, injuring two children and damaging vehicles and shops, according to local authorities.
In March, a drone strike from Sudan killed at least 17 people in the same town, including mourners attending a funeral. President Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno condemned the attack and ordered the military to retaliate against any future strikes originating from Sudan, whether carried out by the Sudanese army or the RSF.
A month earlier, Chad shut its eastern border with Sudan after five soldiers and three civilians were killed in clashes allegedly involving the SAF and RSF. At least 12 others were wounded in the incident, which also occurred in Tine, officials said.

articles.title: Zelensky Meets With Coalition of the Willing Leaders, Says Ukraine Faces $27B Defense Budget Shortfall
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine faces a $27 billion defense budget shortfall, calling for early disbursement of European loan funds.
Zelensky made the remarks in a statement following a meeting with leaders of the Coalition of the Willing hosted in Kyiv, on Monday, Aug. 24, as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day. He said the Defense Ministry had used funds allocated for the end of the year earlier than planned because of the budget’s structure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We now have to operate under funding constraints,” Zelensky said, adding that “one of the main options is to provide funds from the European loan ahead of schedule, already this year.”
Frozen Russian assets
Zelensky said Ukraine must also pursue other ways to finance its defense against Russia’s invasion, pointing to frozen Russian assets held in partner countries, including Europe and Japan.
“Wherever those assets are held, we need to find a fair way to use them to defend against Russia’s war,” Zelensky said.
He also praised the Coalition of the Willing for bringing together countries prepared “not only to talk about security, but to act and build real security together.”
Black Sea corridor
In a follow-up statement, Zelensky said Russia was attempting to disrupt Ukraine’s maritime corridor in the Black Sea, particularly by trying to impose a total blockade.
“Three to four ships still enter and leave Odesa each day, despite Russian strikes on port infrastructure,” Zelensky said, adding that traffic through the corridor had been three to four times higher before Russia began attempting to block the route.
Zelensky: There Is No Doubt – Ukraine Will Always Be Independent
To address the issue, Ukraine is considering several options with allied countries, including a negotiating track with Russia, as well as stronger air defenses for the grain corridor.
The consequences of reciprocated strikes on port infrastructure in the Black Sea continue to disrupt trade far beyond Ukraine’s borders, as reduced Ukrainian agricultural exports drive up food prices globally.
Turkey has experienced repeated stray-drone incidents, along with attacks on Turkish-flagged fishing vessels, and has even called on Russia and Ukraine to take direct measures to ensure navigational safety in the Black Sea.
However, Russia has rejected the idea, with Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova saying Moscow had not received a formal proposal from Turkey. She also warned against “half-measures” that would give Ukraine relief without resolving the wider conflict.
Other EU countries have also faced violations of its airspace by Russian drones.
Romanian military divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones found drifting near the strategic Neptun Deep offshore gas project in the Black Sea on Aug. 11, weeks after the NATO country began shooting down frequent stray drones.
“No country has the right to starve the world,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on July 23, arguing that coordinated international pressure could force Russia to stop the attacks.
Meeting with EU’s Costa, Luxembourg’s Frieden
Separately on Monday, Zelensky met European Council President António Costa, with whom he discussed Ukraine’s defense and economic needs.
Patriot interceptors remain a priority as Ukraine continues to prepare for the upcoming autumn and winter.
“We also discussed how the EU can help Ukrainian exports withstand Russia’s terrorist strikes on ports and agriculture,” Zelensky said. “It is important that we find joint European solutions to all these challenges,” he continued.
Zelensky also met Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden, calling the visit a “strong and much-needed signal” of support for Ukrainians defending the country.
Luxembourg is ready to seek solutions for Ukraine’s Defense Forces funding and the country’s budget shortfall – both bilaterally and through the EU, according to Zelensky.
He thanked the country for its readiness to support humanitarian efforts as well, including the reconstruction of university dormitories. “Above all, this is about our young people and the future of our country,” Zelensky said.
