Ukraine Torches Three Ozon Mega-Warehouses, Hits MiG-29, as Drone Forces Hit 66 Targets in One Night
Ukrainian strike drones hit three major Ozon logistics centers across southern Russia, igniting large fires at facilities with a combined warehouse area of more than 314,000 square meters, according to photos and videos published by the OSINT community Exilenova+ on August 24.
The strikes formed part of a much broader Ukrainian operation deep behind Russian lines. Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said his units successfully engaged 66 Russian targets during the night, including a MiG-29 fighter jet, four radar systems, military facilities and vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Birds of the Unmanned Systems Forces successfully struck 66 enemy targets in the operational depth of the enemy rear on the night of August 24,” Brovdi said.
Among the most significant targets, according to the commander, was another Russian MiG-29 near Dolotinka in Russia’s Rostov region.
“Among the sensitive targets was another MiG-29 [Dolotinka, Rostov region, Russia] and four radar systems: two Kasta-2E2 units, a Nebo-SV radar [all in Russia’s Rostov region] and an ST-68 radar [Rozdolne, Crimea],” Brovdi said.
He also reported the destruction of a base used by Russia’s SOBR special police forces in occupied Strilkove in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as strikes against energy infrastructure across Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.
Two vessels associated with Russia’s shadow fleet—a tanker and a bulk carrier—were also hit in the Black Sea, Brovdi said. Eleven Russian temporary deployment points were struck across occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Three Ozon logistics centers were among the most visible targets of the overnight campaign.
The largest was a warehouse complex near Tyube in Russia’s Dagestan region, covering approximately 130,000 square meters. The site serves as a major logistics hub for northern Dagestan and lies roughly 800 to 900 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
A major fire erupted following the strike, with local residents reporting that the glow from the blaze could be seen from as far as 10 kilometers away.
Another Ozon logistics center was targeted in Nevinnomyssk, in Russia’s Stavropol region. The facility covers approximately 93,514 square meters.
The third site was an Ozon warehouse near Enem in Adygea, close to the border with Russia’s Krasnodar region. The complex covers about 91,200 square meters. A large fire developed at the facility after the attack.
Ozon is one of Russia’s largest online marketplaces and operates a sprawling logistics network comparable in function to major Western e-commerce platforms.
An investigation earlier found that Russian troops fighting in Ukraine had repeatedly ordered body armor, thermal-imaging equipment, radios, drone batteries, signal boosters, FPV components and payload-release systems through Ozon. Drone-related products were ordered through Ozon particularly frequently.
Ukraine has already put seven of the ten largest logistics centers operated by Russian e-commerce company Wildberries, OZON rival, out of operation.
Wildberries facilities in Domodedovo and at the Koledino industrial park were among the sites affected. The Koledino facility, covering approximately 250,000 square meters, was the company’s largest warehouse by area.

articles.title: Ozon was the big winner from Wildberries’ ruin. Five weeks later, it’s the target of Ukraine’s drone attacks.
articles.body:
Ozon was the big winner from Wildberries’ ruin. Five weeks later, it’s the target of Ukraine’s drone attacks.
For a third straight night, Ukraine’s military has struck warehouses belonging to the Russian online marketplace Ozon. The first drone strike, overnight on August 22, targeted the company’s warehouse in Chapaevsk (Samara region); the building caught fire and several people were injured. Ukrainian forces attacked a warehouse in Orenburg overnight on August 23. Overnight on August 24, warehouses in Adygeysk (Adygea), Nevinnomyssk (Stavropol Krai), and Makhachkala (Dagestan) came under attack. Fires broke out at most of the sites, and people were injured.
Ozon’s shares on the Moscow Exchange fell 28% as the strikes continued, then recovered part of the loss. The independent Russian outlet Agentstvo calculated that Ukrainian forces struck roughly 233,000 square meters (2.5 million square feet) of storage over the three days — or 6% of Ozon’s total warehouse space. At the end of 2025, the company had 50 full-cycle fulfillment centers that process goods from intake to shipment and more than 150 delivery hubs, with warehouses covering about 5 million square meters (53.8 million square feet).
Ukrainian forces began striking Ozon five weeks after they started hitting warehouses belonging to the Russian online marketplace Wildberries. The Wildberries campaign began on July 18. Journalists and analysts have counted 23 Wildberries warehouses damaged or destroyed, at least 14 people killed, and more than 100 injured. Wildberries lost up to 40% of its warehouse space, and total losses for the company and its sellers are estimated in the hundreds of billions of rubles (billions of dollars).
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has openly named Ozon its new target. “After Ukrainian units struck Wildberries’ 15 largest logistics hubs, now it’s Ozon’s turn,” the ministry said on August 22. It called the attacks on Russian marketplaces “long-range sanctions” and explained the reasoning this way: “Systematic strikes on storage centers for dual-use goods complicate the enemy’s logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had “opened Pandora’s box” when it began attacking Russian commercial sites. “Well, then, you’ll get a response targeting your most sensitive economic sectors, which are already on their last legs,” he vowed last week. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov pointed back to those exact words in his own comments on the Ozon strikes: “Kyiv feels the responses every day, every night, and will keep feeling them.”
Ozon had been seen as a beneficiary of the Wildberries crisis — and it was bracing for a crisis of its own. Ozon ranks second in Russian e-commerce, behind Wildberries, and the Ukrainian strikes on the market leader’s warehouses only strengthened Ozon’s position. At the same time, Ozon was trying to prepare for possible Ukrainian strikes: it moved high-value goods out of warehouses and into pickup points, raised insurance rates for sellers, and offered them a sales model that skips warehouse storage. But after the first strikes, some sellers still faulted the company, saying it could have done more to protect itself and them.
The government will help Wildberries. What it will do for Ozon is still unclear. On Putin’s orders, the Finance Ministry drew up a support plan for Wildberries and its sellers, consisting mainly of tax deferrals and the option to pay in installments. Whether the authorities will do the same for Ozon and its sellers is an open question. The Economic Development Ministry has said it is ready to take up the matter if Ozon requests help. Ozon’s management has yet to comment on the Ukrainian attacks, their consequences, or any way out of the crisis.

articles.title: Ex-Pussy Riot member Rita Flores says she cooperated with the FSB for nearly three years before escaping Russia
articles.body:
Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores has stated that in February 2023, officers from the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) coerced her into cooperating with them by using threats of criminal prosecution and physical violence against her and her loved ones. According to Flores, in the years that followed she passed information about artists and political activists to the security service. Then, in the summer of 2025, she received an assignment to help organize the killing of former Mediazona publisher and Pussy Riot member Pyotr Verzilov.
Flores recounted the story in an interview with lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov, who had helped her flee Russia around ten days earlier. In a conversation with The Insider, Zakhvatov said that he learned of Flores’s relationship with the security services in the summer of 2005, and preparations for her evacuation had taken roughly a year.
How the FSB recruited Flores
According to Flores, she was recruited on Feb. 17, 2023, following a search of her Moscow apartment. That day, media reported that her phone and laptop had been seized and a message had been sent from her phone to her lawyer stating that she had been taken to the Investigative Committee. Flores now says that in reality she had remained at home with two FSB officers.
Zakhvatov told The Insider that the recruitment was preceded by prolonged psychological pressure: Flores had been detained multiple times, placed in temporary detention centers, subjected to surveillance, and had her home searched. According to the lawyer, the final search differed from the previous iterations. This time, one of the officers who entered the apartment addressed Flores in a markedly gentle tone before his colleague began applying intense pressure on her.
“First they worked her over psychologically like that, then threatened her into signing one document, then two days later they made her sign another,” Zakhvatov told The Insider.
As the lawyer stresses, Flores already had extensive experience dealing with the security forces. She had taken part in Pussy Riot protests and was detained multiple times. She knew she was being watched, and Zakhvatov himself had previously helped her evade surveillance.
“It’s difficult to say she was completely unprepared. Nevertheless, under certain circumstances, if you find the right approach to a person and hit a vulnerable spot, then, as practice has shown, [recruitment] is possible,” he said.
“Harley”: tracking artists and activists for the FSB
Flores herself recounted that during the process, the officers threatened her with criminal charges over posts she had made about Russian soldiers killing civilians in Bucha, and the officers also made threats about her family members. She was later taken to the security service’s building on Michurinsky Avenue, where she signed cooperation documents. According to Flores, she was given the operational alias “Harley” and was assigned a handler — an FSB officer named Ivan.
Flores’s first assignment, she says, was to compile profiles on contemporary artists from Russia and neighboring countries. She was subsequently required to gather information on potential law enforcement targets, including details about their associates, relatives, habits, and vulnerabilities including drug use, infidelities, and mental health. According to Flores, this data could be used as tools of pressure and blackmail.
Flores claims she tried to sabotage her work by withholding information that could be dangerous to people she knew, and she deliberately cut off contact with individuals whom the FSB assigned her to “develop.” At the same time, according to her, the security service gained access to her phone through surveillance software.
Zakhvatov told The Insider that Flores had indeed tried to avoid carrying out her assignments.
“She tried to wriggle out of things in every way she could. Sometimes it worked, sometimes it didn’t. But fortunately, no one was harmed,” the lawyer said.
Among those she was required to gather information on, Flores named street artist Phillip Kozlov, known as Philippenzo, who in the summer of 2023 created graffiti titled “Izrossilovanie” (a fusion of the words “Russia” and “rape”). Kozlov was later detained, received two consecutive 15-day administrative sentences, and became a subject in a criminal vandalism case. He subsequently left Russia.
The plot to kill Pyotr Verzilov
The most serious assignment, Flores claims, came in the summer of 2025. According to her, FSB officers proposed that she help organize the killing of Pyotr Verzilov, the unofficial spokesperson of Pussy Riot, with whom she had previously been in a relationship. Flores was to lure him to Serbia and arrange a meeting at a predetermined café.
“After that, I was supposed to step outside on some pretext,” Flores said. According to her, the plan was to then abduct and kill Verzilov.
For her participation in the operation, she was allegedly offered a reward of up to 3 million rubles ($36,000). Flores also claims that her handlers repeatedly asked her to find at least a partial image of Verzilov’s house in Ukraine in order to establish his location and place an explosive device nearby.
After receiving the assignment related to Verzilov, Flores reached out to Zakhvatov. They then began working on extricating her from the security service’s control and arranging her departure from Russia.
The lesson for other coerced informants
According to Zakhvatov, one of the key tasks was to recover Flores’s passport. They also initially considered a course of action in which the activist would pretend to agree to take part in the killing of Verzilov in order to create the opportunity for arresting the FSB team on Serbian territory, but the idea was ultimately abandoned.
“It was too dangerous for Rita. And most importantly, the plan lacked credibility. The FSB officers knew very well that Rita and Pyotr had been close. We thought that such a proposal might itself be a provocation on their part, or could trigger a serious loyalty test for Rita, which she most likely would have failed,” Zakhvatov explained.
After that, they focused on preparing the evacuation. The lawyer has declined to disclose how Flores managed to leave Russia.
Flores noted that she received money from the Russian security services in exchange for her cooperation. Initially she was given a one-time payment of 30,000 rubles ($360), and in the final months before her departure, she says, the FSB paid her 50,000 rubles ($600) per month.
Following Flores’s evacuation, Zakhvatov published an appeal to others who may have been recruited by Russian intelligence services and wish to stop cooperating. As the lawyer explained to The Insider, this is not a dedicated evacuation program for informants, so he does not expect a large number of such inquiries. However, according to him, the Flores case has demonstrated the need to create a dedicated communication channel for people in a similar predicament.
“Since this situation has arisen, we need to use it somehow to disrupt the recruiters’ game... If a person has encountered the same problem as Rita did, they can reach out and receive some form of assistance,” Zakhvatov told The Insider.
He left separate contact details for such inquiries on Element X, Telegram, and Proton email while urging people not to contact him from devices known to the Russian security services.
According to Zakhvatov, one of the most important things an informant who has reached safety must do is speak openly about their cooperation with the security service. Keeping this fact secret, the lawyer argues, allows recruiters to continue using it as leverage and compel a person to carry out assignments even after leaving Russia.
“You’ve already been hooked, you’ve already been reeled in, some trace has already been left. That trace means that at any moment — as the recruitment victim understands — you can be held accountable for it and can be forced to do things you don’t want to do... It’s important that people don’t stay silent,” Zakhvatov told The Insider.
According to the lawyer, this is precisely why it was important to make Flores’s full story public — detailing the methods that FSB officers allegedly used on her.
“People need to know about all these methods; they need to be publicized so that people understand how to handle such a situation correctly and avoid falling into this trap,” he said.
Flores herself also explained her decision to publicly disclose her FSB cooperation as coming from a desire to help others in similar situations.
“I suspect more people have been recruited. And I would like to help them. I am a living example that you can simply reach out to the right people, and they will help you one hundred percent,” she said.

articles.title: Ontario’s premier: Canada should be ready to cut electricity, critical minerals as trade woes worsen
articles.body:
Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, official tells AP
TORONTO (AP) — Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday, an official familiar with the plans told The Associated Press, escalating a trade fight that has sharply worsened since negotiations with the Trump administration collapsed.
The official spoke Monday on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the plans publicly.
Prime Minister Mark Carney had said Saturday that retaliation would target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, but he said Monday that Canada may instead use more targeted measures.
President Donald Trump escalated the dispute again Monday, telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than tariffs already imposed and threatening new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel.
Earlier Monday, Carney accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada and said U.S. trade demands had confirmed Canada’s fears that the United States was seeking to dismantle major Canadian industries.
“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said.
He said Canada was willing to resume talks when Washington returned with “the right attitude.”
Carney was blunter in French.
“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”
The fiery words from both sides show how U.S.-Canada relations have deteriorated since Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, triggering the president’s threatened 50% tariffs the next day on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Carney cast doubt on the U.S.'s dependability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.”
Trump unleashes personal attacks on Canadian leaders
On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada’s auto industry beginning next year.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticizing what he called the country’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.
Carney said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production.
“This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-U.S. industry.
Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure.
“We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”
Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and once again referring to Canada’s prime minister as “Governor Carney.”
Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.”
Ford is a Progressive Conservative whose party differs from that of Carney, a Liberal, but the two underscore broad political unity in Canada over the trade fight with Trump.
Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity
Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario.
Critical minerals are increasingly important to U.S. national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.
Ford said Canada should also consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south.
“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”
Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides backed away.
Auto industry becomes a central battleground
Ford accused Trump of not simply seeking a better trade deal but aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.
Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state.
“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said.
The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the center of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other U.S. states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production.
Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump’s new threat of a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the center of the escalating dispute.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
Ford says he opposed preliminary deal
Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from negotiations, and that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement.
“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.”
Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty.
Carney said the dispute also exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, saying protections for French and Canadian culture that Washington views as trade irritants are considered fundamental rights in Canada.
“Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”
___
Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed from Washington.

articles.title: Israel steps up attacks on Syria hours after top Syrian diplomat meets Mossad chief
articles.body:
Israel steps up attacks on Syria hours after top Syrian diplomat meets Mossad chief
TEHRAN — Before dawn on Monday, six Israeli armored vehicles and an infantry company crossed into western Daraa, sweeping homes in the Syrian village of Ma’ariya under hovering surveillance drones before withdrawing back across the occupied Golan frontier.
Hours later, another Israeli unit moved into southern Quneitra, raiding the village of Sayd al-Hanout after detaining a local shepherd near al-Rafid the day before. The ground advances coincided with a blast near Palmyra’s regional directorate.
The raids unfolded hours after the top diplomat of the Ahmad “al-Jolani” al-Sharaa government, Asaad al-Shaibani, sat across from Mossad Director Roman Gofman in Jordan, according to reports from Axios and AFP.
The U.S.-mediated meeting was advertised as an effort to lower regional temperatures following an August 18 Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib.
Instead, the rapid sequence of military operations demonstrated the stark reality on the ground: the so-called diplomatic negotiations in Amman have done nothing to halt Israeli troop movements inside Syria.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights documented seven Israeli ground incursions across Daraa and Quneitra within a single 24-hour window on Monday.
Local monitors counted over 60 military violations between August 15 and August 21 alone, ranging from land-leveling and surveillance camera installations to makeshift military checkpoints.
Rather than isolated raids, these operations form a continuous campaign to carve out operational freedom deep inside Syrian territory.
Air operations follow the same aggressive logic. The August 18 attack on Abu al-Duhur involved eight separate waves of strikes targeting runways and storage facilities.
Israeli officials claimed the strike pre-empted a Turkish military buildup at the base. Both Ankara and Damascus denied the existence of any such deployment, while U.S. Special Envoy Tom Barrack called the bombing “an unnecessary escalation.”
Yet, days after briefly announcing a pause in contacts over the incident, al-Shaibani traveled to Jordan to discuss a proposed U.S.-supervised special operations room supposedly meant to deconflict Israeli, Turkish, and Syrian military movements.
Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has framed the new political reality in Damascus as a strategic opportunity.
Tel Aviv unilaterally voided the 1974 disengagement agreement, seized Mount Hermon, and established forward outposts in the buffer zone.
Roughly 80 percent of subsequent Israeli air strikes have hit Quneitra, Daraa, and Damascus, aiming to keep Syria’s military infrastructure dismantled.
Accommodation has brought the “al-Jolani” al-Sharaa government no security.
In Jordan, the Syrian side reportedly insisted on a full Israeli withdrawal to pre-December 2024 lines and reaffirmed its right to rebuild a national army.
Tel Aviv treats negotiations as a stall tactic to solidify its presence on the ground, while Washington brokers talks without placing boundaries on Israel’s aggressive maneuvers.

articles.title: Russia Proposes Tax Relief for Wildberries Following Ukrainian Drone Attacks
articles.body:
The Russian government has drafted tax relief measures for Wildberries and its sellers following Ukrainian drone attacks on the retailer’s warehouses and logistics centers.
The proposal would defer tax and insurance payments, freeze tax audits, and ease “administrative pressure” on businesses that suffered major losses, according to Russia’s Finance Ministry on Monday, Aug. 24.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The measures would apply to sellers whose losses exceed 5% of their annual revenue, in which case they would receive a 12-month deferral on value-added tax (VAT), corporate tax, and other liabilities due between August 2026 and July 2027.
Proposed tax deferrals
After the grace period, affected Wildberries sellers would be allowed to clear the deferred liabilities through monthly installments over a further 12 months.
According to The Moscow Times, a similar arrangement would be available to Wildberries & Russ (RWB) – the parent company of the e-commerce platform – with payment deadlines deferred until July 28, 2027, followed by a year-long installment plan.
The relief proposal has been sent to the Russian cabinet for final approval by Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
The Moscow Times reported that the measures follow instructions from Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who directed federal agencies and the Central Bank to organize emergency support for Wildberries and related businesses.

Ukraine inflicts heavy damage to Wildberries
The measures follow weeks of Ukrainian strikes on Wildberries’ logistics infrastructure.
At least 23 company facilities have been targeted since mid-July, with products worth an estimated 480 billion rubles (roughly $5.7 billion) destroyed or damaged, according to Data Insight analysts cited by The New York Times on Aug. 8.
According to the same Data Insight estimate, Wildberries has lost around one-third of its warehouse space following repeated Ukrainian drone strikes.
“Wildberries has almost run out of its biggest warehouses,” Data Insight analyst Sergei Semko told The New York Times. “Every single day one warehouse after another is getting methodically destroyed.”
Tens of thousands of businesses have been affected. Separately, Reuters reported that at least 1.18 million square meters (292 acres) of Wildberries warehouse space had been damaged or destroyed. That amounts to more than one-fifth of its total capacity.
One Moscow-based source told Reuters that his deliveries had fallen from around 400 parcels a day to about 150, adding that he was trying to sell his business.
Ukraine has described Wildberries as a legitimate target due to them selling products with possible military use, such as first-person-view (FPV) drones and fiber-optic cables.
Wildberries, however, denied supplying Russia’s armed forces, saying weapons and military equipment are prohibited from sale on its marketplace.
The company accounts for around 10% of Russian retail sales, making it a significant contributor to Russia’s wartime economy.

articles.title: Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
articles.body:
Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Drug gangs and rebel groups in Colombia are increasingly recruiting children and using them to perform potentially lethal tasks that include piloting explosives-laden drones, Human Rights Watch said in a report published Monday.
The international watchdog said criminal organizations in the South American country often use social media to recruit children as they try to assert control over rural areas where they profit from the drug trade, extortion and illegal mining.
“Armed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “Protection systems are failing, and social media platforms have become a more effective recruiting ground.”
Child recruitment is on the rise again
According to Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ Office, at least 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups since 2021, with 625 cases reported in 2024.
In 1999, during the peak of the conflict between Colombia’s military and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, an estimated 1,320 children were recruited into the fighting, according to a report by a national truth commission.
A 2016 peace deal between Colombia’s government and the FARC rebels reduced violence in many parts of the country and slowed the recruitment of children by armed groups.
But child recruitment is picking up again as smaller rebel groups and other criminal organizations fight over control of rural areas abandoned by FARC guerrillas following the peace deal, where law enforcement and social services continue to be weak.
In Colombia, rebel groups have long used children to perform tasks that include serving as messengers, gathering intelligence, cooking or engaging with the enemy — while girls are sometimes forced into sexual acts with commanders.
The Human Rights Watch report says children are now also being trained in drone warfare, as rebel groups increasingly use drones outfitted with explosives to strike at rival groups or launch attacks on police and army bases.
Human Rights Watch verified videos published on social media that show children using explosives-laden drones, and interviewed family protection officers who work with children who have escaped from armed groups or have been allowed to demobilize.
“Released children who report having operated drones say that armed groups describe the activity as a game rather than as participation in armed fighting,” the report said.
Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ office said in a separate report published Monday that armed groups conducted 121 attacks with drones in the first five months of this year, in which 21 people were killed and 145 were injured.
Social media accounts ‘glorify’ life with rebels
Human Rights Watch identified dozens of social media accounts that “glorify” life in rebel groups, echoing a concern previously voiced by the United Nations.
The watchdog group said in some cases, the algorithms of platforms like Meta and TikTok “appear to have actively promoted” such content that encourages children to join rebel groups.
Meta and TikTok replied to Human Rights Watch saying they prohibit content that promotes violence, and that they had taken down accounts flagged by the organization.
Human Rights Watch also said a FARC holdout group led by a commander known as Ivan Mordisco is involved in most cases of child recruitment and is recruiting heavily in Colombia’s Cauca region.
Nearly half of all recruiting cases reported by Colombian authorities since 2021 involved Indigenous children, according to data analysis by Human Rights Watch, despite Indigenous people making up just 4% of the population.
The watchdog group also said girls made up 40% of all recruited children.
Human Rights Watch called on the Colombian government to devote more resources to prosecuting members of armed groups who recruit children, while stepping up efforts to prevent recruitment in rural areas.
There was no immediate government response to the report.
The organization also called on social media platforms to establish channels where users can easily report content that’s related to the recruitment of children, and preserve evidence that can be made available to prosecutors.

articles.title: Russia grinds up the eastern approach to Sloviansk after its northeastern push stalled
articles.body:
Russian forces have gained ground on the eastern approaches to Sloviansk and continue to prioritize an eastern route toward the city, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW). Their earlier push from the northeast had bogged down, and Russia now aims to set up a future assault on one of the last major cities Ukraine still holds in Donetsk Oblast. A quick move on the city itself remains extremely unlikely, ISW said.
Russia's 2026 summer campaign in the east has advanced through field edges and small villages rather than the breakthroughs the Kremlin keeps promising, the grinding pattern that has defined the fighting across Donetsk Oblast for years.
Kostiantynivka: Why one city in Donbas matters so much that Putin lies about having captured it
The eastern approach
Ukrainian military observer Kostiantyn Mashovets reported that Russian forward units are advancing across several tactical areas at once in the Sloviansk direction. He said the command of Russia's 3rd Combined Arms Army rushes assault infantry forward right after each successful infiltration. Russian troops reached the southeastern edge of Pyskunivka, east of Sloviansk, from the east and northeast, moving off positions they had seized on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets, Mashovets said. Zakitne lies northeast of Pyskunivka and Kryva Luka southeast of it, and ISW read the advance as evidence Russia has consolidated positions in both.
They also infiltrated the southern and southeastern outskirts of Mykolaivka from western Rai-Oleksandrivka. ISW assessed that Russia is running a dual effort to connect its units near Kryva Luka with those at Rai-Oleksandrivka, so it can assault Mykolaivka from dominant terrain to the east and south at once. Mashovets added that other Russian groups slipped through three settlements along the E-40 Bakhmut-Sloviansk highway, trying to hold the western bank of the Siverskyi Donets-Donbas Canal and reach the river just east of the city.
ISW observed reports on 23 August that Ukrainian forces repelled a Russian infiltration attempt in Mykolaivka.
Oleksandr Borodin, spokesperson for Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, said the Lyman direction falls in his corps' zone and that Russia's goal there is to half-encircle the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the flank—first securing bridgeheads across the rivers, then cutting logistics. He called those plans unrealistic:
"We have quite serious defensive positions there and have been preparing for a long time. The capabilities they currently have to try to accomplish this task are insufficient even to come close to achieving such a goal."
Why Moscow switched directions
Russia prioritized attacking Sloviansk from the northeast through Lyman when it opened its spring-summer 2026 offensive, but that effort has largely stalled. The Siverskyi Donets River, which loops north and northeast of the city, together with a web of canals, handed Ukrainian defenders a natural moat. So Russian commanders now treat Mykolaivka as a key prize. Taking it would let them strike west toward Sloviansk from the east, skirting the water obstacles that blocked the northeastern route.
Ukrainian intelligence units will not help: Analyst warns that once Russia breaks into Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, reinforcing them only delays inevitable
A slow road into the Fortress Belt
Sloviansk anchors the northern end of Ukraine's Fortress Belt, a chain of fortified cities that has blunted Russian advances in Donetsk Oblast since 2014. ISW cautioned that Russian forces are extremely unlikely to make fast gains west of Mykolaivka, since they still need to seize several more settlements first.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 23 August that Putin has ordered his army to seize all of Donetsk Oblast by 31 December. By ISW's count, it is the 15th such deadline since 2022, and Russia has missed every one that has come due.
Zelenskyy put Russia's frontline casualties this year at around 267,000, including about 155,000 killed, and said 70% to 80% of them fall in the Kostiantynivka direction. Russia holds about 79.89% of Donetsk Oblast, by ISW's count, and Zelenskyy said the Kremlin is preparing to mobilize around 300,000 men after the 18–20 September State Duma elections, partly to reinforce Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.

US sanctions Chinese entities, issues global warning on ‘Economic D-Day’ against Iran
Washington warns Iran-linked entities face removal from US dollar system as Trump presses world leaders to cut financial ties
The United States on Monday announced fresh sanctions against 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong, and issued a warning demanding “immediate action” from nations maintaining economic and commercial ties with Iran.
The measures are part of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to choke off Tehran economically after military strikes and diplomatic negotiations failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the six-month-long conflict.
Dubbed “Economic D-Day” by the Trump administration, the new actions aim to expand Washington’s secondary sanctions, putting entities in multiple jurisdictions on notice.
“Let me be clear: any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking,” said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent at a press conference.
Bessent added that US President Donald Trump is “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests” to halt their engagement with the Iranian regime, but did not identify the countries he had contacted.
The campaign’s effectiveness may ultimately depend on how far Washington is willing to press China, Iran’s most important remaining economic partner.

articles.title: The oil market now ignores Trump’s messages
articles.body:
The oil market now ignores Trump’s messages
Kayhan, in an article, examined Trump’s desperation in the current situation. Trump’s frustration and anger come at a time when Axios acknowledged that changes in oil prices in response to Trump’s social‑media posts about the Iran war have steadily declined over time.
Fluctuations in oil prices ripple across the US and global economies, and the conflict has caused unprecedented disruption in supply. In the early weeks, markets overreacted to many of Trump’s posts. But for months now, the market has been ignoring them, because they do not reflect reality and have no connection to the number of barrels actually leaving the Strait of Hormuz. The erosion of Trump’s influence over oil markets carries political consequences, as Democrats use energy prices as a cudgel against Republicans in the midterm elections. In the first few months, the White House was highly successful in controlling the narrative and pushing prices down — but it has now lost that leverage.
Ettelaat: Maintaining good relations with neighbors is essential for Iran
Ettelaat evaluated the Mecca Pact. Although Iran currently has no tension with Turkey or Pakistan, it is possible that under certain circumstances — and with Saudi financial assistance to these two countries combined with US provocation — tensions could emerge. For this reason, Tehran need not be overly sensitive about the Mecca Pact. If the pact adopts a strongly oppositional stance toward Israel, it would be an opportunity for Tehran. If it remains indifferent toward Israel but shows sensitivity toward Iran, it becomes a threat. The Mecca Pact could, at a critical moment, be inflamed by Riyadh and Washington, clouding Iran’s relations with Ankara and Islamabad. In any case, it is better for Iran to keep its good relations with its neighbors strong and to further reinforce them, while remaining highly alert and prepared for all possible scenarios, risks, and breaches of commitment, even in the worst case.
Arman-e-Emrooz: A challenging situation
Arman-e-Emrooz assessed the intensification of US sanctions and the naval blockade of Iran through three possible scenarios. Amid these developments, it appears that one of the three scenarios will soon unfold. One possibility is that the Trump administration steps back and announces progress in negotiations, meaning the harsh sanctions will not be implemented. The second scenario is that the plan is announced and executed, but after a short period it is quietly set aside as both sides show flexibility and a negotiation process begins. The third possibility is that the severe economic sanctions continue until the US midterm elections and are then accompanied by military strikes to reshape the situation on the ground. Each of these three scenarios has its supporters, but two factors strongly influence them: first, the degree of firmness on current positions; and second, the election results soon to be held in the US and Israel.
Shargh: A crisis in the global economy
Shargh, in an analysis, examined the global economic crisis triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The flight of oil tankers from the strait amid escalating military tensions has pushed shipping rates to more than four times their pre‑war levels. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has now become a crisis for the global economy. This unprecedented surge in transport costs brings a chain of negative consequences. First, the final cost of oil for consumer countries has risen sharply, meaning greater pressure on household budgets and intensified inflation worldwide. Second, countries lacking sufficient strategic reserves face serious challenges in securing their required oil and may encounter fuel shortages. Third, higher transport costs raise the final price of essential goods and industrial raw materials, since oil plays a key role in the production and transport of many products. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has imposed a full‑scale economic crisis on the world — one that affects all countries, from major importers to ordinary consumers.
Resalat: Disrupting the Arab–American coalition‑building game
American strategists openly speak of efforts to unite the Persian Gulf Arab states against Iran. Our diplomacy must anticipate the adversary’s moves and deprive them of the pretexts for coalition‑building. The agreement to restore relations with Saudi Arabia, along with expanding ties with the UAE and Qatar, must be upgraded from a mere political truce to deep economic and security linkages. If the Persian Gulf states develop tightly interwoven commercial and economic interests with Iran, they will not easily play Washington’s anti‑Iran puzzle. We must show our neighbors that regional security is unified and indivisible. Any provision of bases to the United States or the Israeli regime for actions against Iran’s interests endangers the security and investment climate of the entire region.
At the same time, proposing non‑aggression pacts and cooperation for securing maritime navigation neutralizes the pretext for foreign fleets to remain present.

He emphasized that if the strait is truly under American control, they should demonstrate their presence in the region and prove on the ground what they claim.
Mohebbi noted: Before the war, at least 30 to 40 US warships were present in the Persian Gulf, but today not even a single American warship is in the Persian Gulf. US military assets are currently positioned at least about 400 kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: US could carry out further strikes on Iran if needed: Hegseth
articles.body:
Ahmet Salih Alacaci
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday that Washington is not ruling out further military strikes on Iran, even as the Trump administration intensifies economic pressure on Tehran.
Asked whether kinetic strikes were currently on pause, Hegseth said: “No. If we need to use kinetic strikes, we'll use them.”
“If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the American military, we'll do what we need to do,” he told reporters after a speech to defense industrial workers in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, where he urged US defense contractors to "pivot to a wartime footing."
Hegseth said economic pressure was currently hurting Iran the most but added that the US was “by no means” ruling out strikes “anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran.”
He also claimed the US maintains control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying Washington’s blockade was “ironclad” and that Iran was unable to move oil through the waterway, while the US could protect shipping.
Hegseth said the administration expected Congress to provide the full $1.5 trillion sought for defense, even if approval came during a lame-duck session after November midterm elections but before the newly elected Congress takes office in January.
Asked whether munitions purchases could be cut if the full amount was not approved, he called them “pretty sacred,” saying the Pentagon had entered long-term agreements aimed at increasing supplies of some priority munitions two-, three- or fourfold.
Hegseth also declined to discuss reports that US stocks of ATACMS long-range missiles had been significantly depleted in ongoing conflicts, saying the military had “plenty” available.
- USS Abraham Lincoln heading home
Hegseth also confirmed that the USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home after an extended deployment.
“To the sailors and families of the Lincoln, I say godspeed on a historic mission. Congratulations, you're on your way home,” he said, describing the deployment as “tough” and longer than most.
The Lincoln has spent more than eight months without making a port call, setting a US Navy record. Families of sailors have reported worsening conditions and morale aboard the carrier, though Hegseth has said such claims have been “completely misrepresented.”

articles.title: US launches Operation Economic Outcast to sever Iran's financial 'lifelines'
articles.body:
Muhammed Yasin Güngör

 The US on Monday launched Operation Economic Outcast, a sweeping campaign intended to completely isolate Iran from the global financial system, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced.
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told reporters. 
The US is "no longer managing the Iranian threat" but rather "ending it,” Bessent said, adding that the "strength of America's economy" enabled Washington to conduct such a financial offensive alongside military operations.
Directed by US President Donald Trump, the “unprecedented” sanctions target Iran’s "most vital lifelines," including aviation, shipping, gold, technology, and digital assets, he said.
Bessent also noted that the Treasury was blacklisting more than 60 entities, individuals, and vessels worldwide, significantly broadening secondary sanctions risks for any international party continuing to conduct business with Tehran.
He characterized the policy as the “economic asphyxiation of this regime.”
'No one is above the reach of US sanctions'
 
Bessent warned actors involved in the "ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money" that they would be targeted and "have no one to blame but themselves," emphasizing that "no one was above the reach" of the new measures. 
He also called on US partners to act, saying it was "no longer acceptable to operate in the gray spaces" of the conflict. Bessent said joint teams from the Treasury, State Department and military were meeting with counterparts around the world to deliver a clear message: every country has a "defined timeline" to shut down identified Iranian activities or face unilateral US action.
Also on China, Bessent said "the best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy," adding that the US was currently "level setting" expectations with Beijing.
Bessent also described the United Arab Emirates’ recent decision to halt all trade and financial transactions with Iran as "causal" and a result of US pressure. 
He said Treasury officials had mapped "every node, every facilitator, and every network" used by Tehran for oil smuggling and sanctions evasion. Bessent said the US was pursuing a "zero leakage approach," with "no minimal breathing space" for Iran to rebuild its capabilities as agencies "tighten the noose" on all revenue sources. 
Bessent warned that any entity facilitating money laundering for Tehran will be permanently removed from the US dollar system. 
"I would expect that you will see a major announcement of a financial institution being sanctioned by the end of this week," he further said without elaborating. 
Trump is reportedly making personal phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to terminate interactions with the regime. "We are already seeing results," said Bessent.
“Those who stand with the United States will reap the rewards of our partnership,” Bessent added, warning that those who do not will share in the isolation of a "withering regime." 
The offensive, which Bessent characterized as an "economic D-Day," follows claims from the administration that Iran’s military and nuclear infrastructure have been dismantled.
Trump recently asserted that Tehran is facing 350% inflation and can no longer pay its security forces.

articles.title: International competition launched to design Minab school martyrs’ memorial
articles.body:
International competition launched to design Minab school martyrs’ memorial
TEHRAN – The International Landscape and Memorial Space Design Competition for the Minab School Martyrs’ Cemetery has been officially launched, seeking to create a lasting memorial space that honors the victims, preserves their stories and conveys a message of peace and resistance.
The competition, titled “Architecture; Beyond Consolation — for Peace and Life,” was introduced during a press conference held at the Malek National Library and Museum on Monday, where organizers outlined the objectives, design approach and procedures of the international call.
According to Saeid Mehrpouya, director of the competition, the project follows a decision by the custodian of Astan Quds Razavi to address the site and ultimately construct the memorial. The initiative was also proposed within the legal and planning framework of Iran’s Supreme Council of Urbanism and Architecture.
Mehrpouya said the organizers deliberately chose an open competition format to allow architects and consultants from different backgrounds to participate and to ensure that the project would not be confined to a predetermined design.
“The subject is not limited to designing a particular structure. We want architects and designers to engage with the social and human dimensions of the event and develop a space that can convey its deeper meaning,” he explained.
The competition focuses on a memorial site of about 8,000 square meters in Minab, where the tragic event left a profound impact on families and the wider community.
Mehrpouya said that during visits to Minab, the organizers encountered a site whose physical appearance itself had become part of the collective memory of the tragedy. The school where the incident occurred is planned to be transformed into a museum, while the burial site constitutes another important part of what the organizers describe as a wider memorial chain.
The overall concept includes four interconnected elements: the school that witnessed the tragedy, the burial site, other memorial manifestations of the victims, and a plan to establish eight schools across the country bearing the names of the children.
The competition itself represents the second link in this chain.
According to Mehrpouya, research conducted during visits to the site and examination of accounts surrounding the incident revealed a broader story of innocence and victimhood. The organizers also collected stories about the children, their teachers, their parents, the school bus driver and other individuals connected with the school.
Mehrpouya emphasized that the burial ground cannot be understood simply as a cemetery. For many families, he said, the site has become an extension of their homes and a place where they come to feel close to their children, talk to them and share their grief.
“This is a different kind of space,” he said, adding that the responsibility of the participating architects is to discover the stories embedded in the site and transform them into a tangible and perceptible spatial experience.
The organizers have defined the design process around several stages, beginning with the tragedy itself. They argue that although the catastrophe occurred in a single moment, its consequences continue in the lives of survivors, families and the city.
The second stage concerns the victims themselves and the task of creating a physical space for something that did not previously exist. The architects are expected to address not only the memorialization of the victims but also the transformation of an ordinary piece of land into a place that narrates their deaths, the suffering of their families and the collective trauma of Minab and Iran.
The organizers have also given the competition an international dimension. Mehrpouya said that memorials for victims of major tragedies are not exclusively national phenomena and that the issue of responsibility surrounding such events has attracted international attention.
He stressed that the architectural response should go beyond consolation and address the future as well.
The concept of peace adopted by the competition, he explained, does not signify surrender. Rather, it represents resistance to humiliation and violence. “We did not start the war and we are deeply committed to peace, but we stand against tyranny and brutality,” he said, stressing that the memory of the victims should remain alive for future generations.
The competition's organizers believe the site also represents a form of trauma for survivors. Although the school has been destroyed, memories of the bombing continue to recur in the minds of those who witnessed or survived the event. The memorial, therefore, is expected to contribute to transforming the site into a place where memory can be preserved while creating a sense of calm and continuity.
A visual identity has also been developed for the competition. Its main elements include birds and a drop of blood, with an uncolored, hollow bird serving as the symbol of Makan Nasiri, a missing martyr.
The competition's official call will be published following the press conference on the dedicated website, Minabmemorial.ir, in Persian, English, Arabic, Russian, French, Spanish and Chinese. The website includes the names and ages of the victims, as well as accounts related to their lives, in an effort to provide participants with a deeper understanding of the subject.
The organizers said information about the competition has also been sent to Iran’s cultural and diplomatic representatives in several countries.
The competition offers a total of 24 billion rials in prizes. Five leading entries will receive awards, while eight additional projects will be recognized. In total, 13 selected designs will be honored.
An international jury is being formed, with organizers currently negotiating with several potential international jurors. The final composition of the jury is expected to be announced in the coming weeks. The panel will include three Iranian academic architects and two international architects, representing different generations of professionals.
After the jury selects the top 20 to 30 proposals, the organizers plan to submit them to specialists from other disciplines for multidisciplinary review and expert feedback.
Mehrpouya stressed that the competition will not end with the announcement of the winning design. Instead, the selected proposal will move into the contracting and construction stages, making the competition part of a larger process aimed at creating a physical memorial.
The winning and selected designs will also be compiled into a book and will go on display in different exhibtions, allowing the public to experience the different architectural interpretations of the tragedy and the message of the memorial.
Registration for the competition will begin next week through the official website and will be free of charge. Participants will have 10 weeks to prepare their proposals, followed by a 10-day evaluation period. The competition is expected to conclude in late November, with organizers hoping to complete part of the memorial project before the anniversary of the tragedy in February.
The competition's guidelines have been designed in two sections: the first presents the story and context of Minab, while the second sets out the competition's rules and requirements.
Organizers said they hope the project will ultimately create a memorial landscape unlike existing examples in Iran and elsewhere, transforming a site of profound loss into a place where memory, mourning, resistance, peace and hope for future generations can coexist.
The US-Israeli missile strike on Minab’s Shajareh Tayyebeh Girls’ School and Rahpouyan-e Khalij-e Fars Boys’ School on February 28 left a deep scar on the city. The attack struck shortly before 11 a.m., when students were attending classes. A second missile hit a prayer hall where students had gathered after the initial strike. Rescue and identification operations continued for days, followed by the burial of the victims.
SAB/

articles.title: Palestinian killed in Israeli airstrike on central Gaza: sources
articles.body:
GAZA/JERUSALEM, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A Palestinian was killed and several others wounded in an Israeli airstrike on the Gaza Strip on Monday.
Local sources and eyewitnesses said that an Israeli drone fired a missile at a tent sheltering displaced people in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza.
Medical sources identified the deceased as Mohammed Abu Asad, without elaborating on his identity.
In a separate statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) confirmed the death of Asad, identifying him as a member of Hamas' elite Nukhba force and alleging he took part in the Oct. 7, 2023 attack on southern Israel.
A second militant was also struck in the overnight attack, the IDF added, without disclosing his identity or condition.
The military claimed both had been planning attacks against Israeli troops and civilians and were attempting to rebuild Hamas capabilities while violating the ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the Hamas-run Gaza government media office said in a statement that the Israeli army had committed 4,379 violations of the ceasefire agreement since it took effect in October 2025, resulting in 1,286 deaths, 4,257 injuries, and 180 arrests. ■

articles.title: Darline Graham is no Lindsey, and it’s probably a good thing for America
articles.body:
Darline Graham is no Lindsey, and it’s probably a good thing for America
Appointing Darline Graham to simply finish her brother Lindsey’s Senate term was one thing, but having her run for the next term, with Donald Trump’s support, is simply bonkers. Or does Trump know something we don’t?
Darline’s political inexperience was on full display during last week’s debate against her run-off opponent, Rep. Ralph Norman, when she was unable to answer an elementary question on national security involving China and Taiwan.
Graham was simply asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the US. Incredibly, she even failed to at least respond with a “yes” or “no.”
Clearly unprepared for the big night, Graham began by requesting for the question to be repeated. It didn’t help her. Following the second reading she admitted defeat, saying, “I’m just going to be honest here – I’m not, on national security, that – I’m not that informed on national security. So...”
After her voice quivered for a moment amid rumbling from the debate audience, Graham dug her hole deeper with a non sequitur: “But I do support the military. My brother was in the Air Force for 33 years, so I will do everything I can to support the military. My dad was in the army.”
But things only got worse for poor Darline, who proceeded to admit to her severe shortcomings and incompetency. “I’m not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing – not my area of expertise – but I do support the military.” Some people may think that it is a bit perplexing and not a little scary that Graham is already serving in the Senate on an interim basis.
Following Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sudden death on July 11, Gov. Henry McMaster appointed his sister Darline to finish up the remaining months of his tenure. What began as a sentimental gesture inexplicably morphed into a White House endorsement, with Trump pushing the inexperienced woman to enter the primary race with a chance at serving a six-year term that will begin in January. Feelings for her brother aside, Darline Graham has never held an elected office. Until this summer, she was commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, and earlier held a communications role in the South Carolina Vocational Rehabilitation Department.
Trump’s endorsement notwithstanding, Graham only received 33% of the vote in the special August 11 ballot, forcing her into an August 26 runoff against Ralph Norman, who came in second place with 25% of the vote. “Her lackluster showing reflected South Carolina Republicans’ deep unease with Trump trying to turn one of their Senate seats into an inheritance for someone with a joke of a political resume,” ZeroHedge quipped.
Darline’s egregious debate failure drew comparisons to Miss South Carolina’s famous response to a question in the 2007 Miss Teen USA pageant.
The question she was asked to answer went as follows: “Recent polls have shown a fifth of Americans can’t locate the US on a world map. Why do you think this is?”
The cringe answer: “I personally believe that US Americans are unable to do so because some people out there in our nation don’t have maps. And, I believe that our education like such as in South Africa and the Iraq everywhere like such as... And I believe that they should – our education over here in the US should help the US or should help South Africa and should help the Iraq and the Asian countries, so we will be able to build up our future for our children.”
It is an apt comparison and it would be funny if we weren’t dealing with a position that has the power to actually influence America’s foreign policy.
Having driven her own performance off a cliff, the next day Graham attempted to cover her losses by admitting to Trump attack dog Sean Hannity that she “tripped up on one question.” Brushing aside the importance of her inability to answer the question, Graham told Hannity, “I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician, I don’t speak politician.”
In a separate interview with reporters, Graham said: “I tripped up on one question last night, regarding Taiwan. I don’t speak politician. I was just honest. Of course, Taiwan is our friend. But I think people in South Carolina are more worried about boys in girls’ sports.” Too bad Darline didn’t say that on the debate stage.
With feelings for politicians at an all-time low, it would be a safe bet that the majority of South Carolina Republicans don’t want Graham to “speak politician.” With that said, however, it’s reasonable to expect her to have the capacity to string together some intelligent comments with regards to one of world’s major hot spots, especially at a time when the US Department of War has expended a hefty proportion of its weapons in Iran – a military disaster with no resolution in sight.
Thus, perhaps it can be argued that Darline Graham’s embarrassing lack of knowledge over foreign affairs might be just what the MAGA camp wants – a lot less Lindsey and much more Darline. They may be willing to forgive Darline’s inability to find Taiwan on a map so long as she focuses congressional attention on critical domestic issues, like LGBTQ curricula in schools, soaring costs, and crumbling infrastructure.
On Tuesday, South Carolina Republicans will cast a vote that either continues in the blood-soaked shoes of Lindsey Graham or opts for a change in the person of his sister that keeps the attention on the American homeland.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: UK approves handover of Storm Shadow production technology to Ukraine
articles.body:
UK approves handover of Storm Shadow production technology to Ukraine
The UK has approved the handover of technology for producing Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles to Ukraine.
Source: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv on 24 August
Details: Burnham noted that the UK was one of the first countries to provide Ukraine with long-range weapons in 2023.
He said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had requested access to the UK's Storm Shadow technology so that Ukraine could develop the capability independently. He confirmed that he has approved the request and that British and French defence companies will now work with Ukraine to develop the technology.
The missile is manufactured by European defence company MBDA. According to the company, SCALP – known as Storm Shadow in the UK – is a long-range air-to-surface cruise missile designed for precision strikes on fixed, heavily protected targets, including hardened bunkers and key infrastructure.
According to MBDA, the missile can be used day or night in all weathers. Its guidance system combines inertial navigation, GPS and terrain-referenced navigation. After launch, the missile flies at low altitude to avoid detection. As it approaches its target, an onboard infrared seeker compares the target with a pre-loaded reference image to ensure a precision strike.
Background:
- Burnham arrived in Kyiv on 24 August on his first overseas visit since taking office. He was expected to announce the handover to Kyiv of secret data on British components for the long-range Storm Shadow/SCALP missile "as Ukraine and France look to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine".
- The decision also complements the UK's Project Brakestop, which aims to rapidly develop low-cost long-range strike capabilities for Ukraine.
- In June, Mykhailo Fedorov, the then Ukrainian defence minister, said that Kyiv was negotiating with France to obtain a licence to manufacture SCALP cruise missiles.

articles.title: Ex-Pussy Riot member says FSB coerced her into three years of informing on Russian artists and activists, then told her to help kidnap and kill Pyotr Verzilov
articles.body:
Ex-Pussy Riot member says FSB coerced her into three years of informing on Russian artists and activists, then told her to help kidnap and kill Pyotr Verzilov
Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores (real name Margarita Konovalova) said she began cooperating with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) in 2023, helping the agency gather information on contemporary artists and political activists, including members of Pussy Riot.
Flores described her work for the FSB in an interview with defense attorney Dmitry Zakhvatov, who helped her leave Russia. The outlet Port published both a video and a written summary of the interview.
She met an FSB officer named Ivan — the man who would become her handler — after agents searched her apartment on February 17, 2023. At the time, she was reported to have gone missing after the search. While others searched for her, she was at home with two FSB officers, who coerced her into cooperating. They threatened her with criminal prosecution, said they would kill her relatives, and warned that she herself would “disappear without a trace” if she refused to work for them.
The FSB gave Flores the code name “Harley,” began training her “as an agent,” confiscated all of her documents except her internal Russian passport, and issued her a “work” phone.
Her main job for the FSB was to flag artworks that could give the agency grounds to begin targeting their creators and to compile a “report” on someone the agency planned to prosecute. In that report, she was to lay out the person’s background, relatives and close contacts, habits, and vulnerabilities.
Flores said she took part in the FSB’s targeting of street artist Filipp Kozlov, who works under the name Philippenzo; performance artist Pavel Krisevich; and fellow Pussy Riot member Maria Alyokhina. She said the FSB also tried to enlist her in the kidnapping and murder of Pyotr Verzilov, Mediazona’s former publisher and a member of the art groups Voina and Pussy Riot.
After being handed the Verzilov assignment, Flores contacted Zakhvatov. With his help, she persuaded her handlers to “postpone” the job, then fled the country. Neither she nor Zakhvatov would say how she got out. Flores got in touch with him in the summer of 2025, Zakhvatov said, and she was brought out of Russia about 10 days ago.
Flores said she decided to go public about her work for the FSB to help others in similar situations. On Instagram, she thanked Zakhvatov and former Yukos executive Leonid Nevzlin for their help, saying the two men had “saved her ass and her soul.”
Philippenzo responded to Flores’ statements by sending Meduza an image of a 2017 painting of his that was seized during searches of his studio in 2023.

articles.title: The geopolitical importance of Taiwan and the South China Sea 台灣與南海的地緣政治重要性
articles.body:
Taiwan and the South China Sea have long been major issues in US foreign policy, and tensions involving China have kept both in the news in recent months. Beijing claims Taiwan as its own territory and asserts sovereignty over virtually the entire South China Sea, bringing it into confrontation with US allies and partners in the region.
What happens in Taiwan and the South China Sea could have an impact not only on the region but around the world, given their importance to global trade.
The South China Sea, a large body of water bordered by several nations, including China, the Philippines and Vietnam, is one of the world’s key maritime trade routes. Taiwan produces the majority of the world’s advanced semiconductors.
Photo: Google Map 照片：谷歌地圖
“The two are very much connected,” said Hunter S. Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute in Australia. “If China were to blockade or seek to forcibly retake Taiwan..., the South China Sea could quickly see spillover effects.”
TAIWAN, A KEY ISSUE IN US-CHINA RELATIONS
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that China claims as its own territory, and Beijing has not renounced the use of force to bring it under its control.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
China sends military aircraft, coast guard ships and other vessels around Taiwan on a near-daily basis and periodically conducts large-scale military exercises. Taiwan also regularly holds military drills, including its annual Han Kuang exercises.
The US does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but maintains extensive unofficial relations and is required under US law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
Under that framework, the US has long been Taiwan’s main informal backer and arms supplier, a relationship that has been a persistent source of tensions with Beijing.
TENSIONS PERSIST IN THE SOUTH CHINA SEA
But China asserts sovereignty over much of the South China Sea, despite a 2016 international arbitration ruling that invalidated Beijing’s expansive maritime claims.
In July, on the 10th anniversary of the ruling, the US, the UK and 12 other countries reiterated that China’s expansive claims have no legal basis. Beijing responded by insisting it would neither accept nor recognize the arbitration decision.
Confrontations in the disputed waters have become more frequent in recent years, particularly involving Chinese, Philippine and Vietnamese forces and fishing fleets.
Chinese coast guard ships and other vessels have used powerful water cannons, military-grade lasers and dangerous blocking maneuvers against Philippine forces and fishermen from other claimant countries. Such confrontations have led to collisions at sea and high-risk encounters in the air.
China has also carried out military drills this month near Scarborough Shoal, a disputed area claimed by both China and the Philippines.
In April, the US and the Philippines kicked off the annual Balikatan military exercises. The drills included mock battle scenarios and live-fire exercises in Philippine provinces facing the disputed South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has said that because the South China Sea is one of the world’s most important maritime commercial corridors, “a conflict could cause major disruptions to the flow of trade.” The sea is connected to surrounding waters through several strategic chokepoints, including the Malacca Strait, which links it to the Indian Ocean and the Taiwan Strait, which connects it to the East China Sea.
What would be the main US interests in the region? For Marston, “the primary objective is preventing China from gaining regional hegemony and dominating the Pacific.”
“The security of Taiwan and its allies such as the Philippines, as well as defense of the first island chain, are integral to this overarching goal,” he said.
(AP)
台灣與南海長久以來都是美國外交政策中的重大議題，近數個月來，美中之間的緊張局勢更讓台灣與南海不斷成為新聞焦點。北京宣稱台灣是中國領土的一部分，並對幾乎整個南海主張擁有主權，因而與美國在該區的盟友及夥伴陷入對立。
由於台灣與南海對全球貿易的重要性，此處發生的任何事，不僅可能影響區域局勢，也可能會對全世界造成衝擊。
南海是一片由中國、菲律賓、越南等多國環繞的大型海域，也是全球重要的海上貿易航線之一。台灣則生產全球多數的先進半導體。
澳洲「洛伊國際政策研究所」東南亞計畫主任杭特．S．馬斯頓表示：「台灣與南海有非常密切的關聯。如果中國封鎖台灣，或試圖以武力奪取台灣，南海很快就可能受到外溢效應的影響」。
台灣：美中關係的關鍵議題
台灣是一個自治的民主政體，中國宣稱台灣是其領土的一部分，而北京從未放棄武力犯台的可能性。
中國幾乎每天都派軍機、海警船及其他船隻在台灣周邊活動，並不時舉行大規模軍事演習。台灣也定期舉行軍事演訓，包括每年的漢光演習。
美國與台灣並無正式外交關係，但維持廣泛的非官方關係，而且根據美國法律，美國必須提供台灣自我防衛所需的設備。
在此架構下，美國長期以來一直是台灣主要的非官方支持者與武器供應國，而這樣的關係也一直是美中緊張局勢的緣由之一。
南海緊張局勢持續
另一方面，中國主張對南海大部分海域擁有主權，儘管2016年的國際仲裁案已否定北京對南海範圍廣闊的聲索。
今年7月，在南海仲裁案10週年之際，美國、英國及其他12個國家再次重申，中國對南海廣大範圍的主權主張沒有法律依據。北京則回應稱，既不接受也不承認此仲裁案的裁決。
近年來，南海爭議海域的對峙日益頻繁，尤其是中國、菲律賓與越南的軍警部隊及漁船。
中國海警船及其他船隻曾使用強力水砲、軍用級雷射，以及危險的阻擋與逼近動作，對付菲律賓部隊及其他主權聲索國的漁民。這類對峙已導致海上碰撞，以及空中的高風險接觸。
本月，中國也在黃岩島附近舉行軍事演習。黃岩島是中國與菲律賓均聲稱擁有主權的爭議地區。
今年4月，美國與菲律賓啟動年度「肩並肩」（Balikatan）聯合軍事演習。演習內容包括模擬戰鬥情境及實彈演習，地點位於面向南海爭議海域與台灣海峽的菲律賓省分。
