articles.title: Ukraine got independence as a gift in 1991. Now we pay in blood
articles.body:
In 1991, Ukraine did not shed a drop of blood. It was a transition of power. We raised a flag, we declared ourselves independent, and we received our independence as a gift.
Now we are shedding rivers of blood for real independence.
That is the difference between this Independence Day and the ones before it, and I do not think we have absorbed it yet.
Colonial theory has a name for what happened to us thirty-five years ago. It is called flag independence. You raise the flag, you declare the state, and for a while you believe that was it—that this was the end, and now we simply continue as an independent nation.
In theory it was believed to be like that. In practice, every decolonized nation eventually discovered the same thing: it is not the end. It is the beginning.
The nations that gathered at Bandung in Indonesia in 1955 worked this out before us. They had their flags. They also had the former metropolis still holding the strings—to their economies, their cultures, their political classes. They named it: neocolonialism.
And they understood that real independence would take something longer and harder than a declaration. Not only liberation with arms, but liberation of the mind from the colonial legacy. Not erasing the colonial memory—reworking it, synthesizing it into something new.
So here is the shape of it. Before 1991, Ukrainians waged a struggle for independence without statehood. After 1991, we have been waging a struggle for independence within statehood. The struggle did not end. It changed its conditions.
What was gathered into the Act of Independence
The declaration was a beginning, but it was also a result—of generations.
It begins in the nineteenth century, with people like Taras Shevchenko, who essentially invented a Ukrainian identity. It was a construction. It was not, as Putin claims, the invention of Vladimir Lenin. It was the invention of Ukrainian intellectuals, writers, and religious leaders, who constructed this nation on the basis of what came before—the Cossack Republic, Kyivan Rus, the long stretch from the Middle Ages through early modernity.
Then the dissidents of the Soviet period. Then the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which fought on two fronts against three colonizers: the Germans, the Poles, and the Soviets. Their struggle was clearly anti-colonial. Brutal, but anti-colonial. I do not justify everything they did. I am applying postcolonial theory in order to make sense of what they did, or tried to do. They were defeated. Their ideas resurfaced in 1991 and were gathered into the Act of Independence.
And that Act, while it closed a long period of Ukrainian struggle without a state, opened a new one.
Today, more independence than colonialism
Before 2013, I would say, there was more neocolonialism than independence.
This is a description, not a figure of speech. The former metropolis re-established the strings. Russian capital came into the economy under the presidencies of Leonid Kuchma and Viktor Yanukovych, and Russian corruption came with it.
Proxy parties were planted—the Party of Regions and its various clones. Russian pop music was everywhere, which sounds like a small thing and is not: in postcolonial studies, literature and popular culture are considered among the most effective vehicles of neocolonial control.
Today it is the other way around. Neocolonialism has not evaporated, but the proportion has changed. There is now more independence than neocolonialism—and that itself is what thirty-five years of struggle have achieved.
And corruption was a neocolonial instrument. This is the part Ukrainians resist, so let me put it plainly: our fight against corruption is effectively an anti-colonial fight. In Ukraine people sometimes present this as a dilemma—either we fight corruption or we fight the Russians, we cannot do both. From the perspective of postcolonial studies the dilemma does not exist. Both are anti-colonial efforts. They go hand in hand.
Empires have always travelled with religion on their shoulders, and religion has always helped establish imperial rule in the colonies. In the Ukrainian case it was first the Greek Catholic Church, established in 1596 an instrument of Polish colonization, although this is not the case anymore. But that is how it began.
And presently Russia’s instrument of recolonization is the Moscow Patriarchate, still present in Ukraine as the Ukrainian Orthodox Church under the Moscow Patriarchate (UOC MP).
Anatomy of treason: how the Ukrainian Orthodox Church sold its soul to the “Russian world”
Here I have to say something uncomfortable for many Ukrainians.
Nations that decolonize very often produce new subalterns. In post-colonial language, these are parts of the population that are subdued, oppressed by the dominant power. But we may be producing such subalterns as an effect of pushing back against Russian colonization: groups of Ukrainians belonging to the UOC MP being marginalized, subalternized, by our own struggle. It is a very difficult dilemma how to deal with this subalternization, and I do not have a resolution for it.
Two revolutions against the ratio
Both of Ukraine’s major “Maidan” protests were anti-neocolonial revolutions.
In the Orange Revolution of 2004 and again during the Euromaidan Revolution in 2013, Ukrainians protested because they had decided there was not enough independence—that what we had was more neocolonial than independent, more fake than real, and that the proportion had to be corrected. That is what a Maidan is. A public consensus that the ratio is wrong.
In February 2022, independence very nearly ended. People gave our statehood three days—and not only Russians. That was the opinion of most observers. It did not end. We survived it. But our statehood is still not secured, and it is being secured every day, including today.
What Ukraine contributed to the empire, and how
There is an argument against everything I have said so far, and Ukrainians make it as often as anyone. They object: look, we have contributed to the Russian Empire and to the Soviet one. We have basically built them.
Which is true.
Ukraine helped build the Russian empire. Now it stands in the way of its resurrection – Serhii Plokhii
But Ukrainians were never permitted to contribute as independent agents. They were allowed to contribute exactly as long as they lost their identity—as long as they denounced their own agency. They were contributors without their will and without their identity.
Corsica is my example. It had its own culture, its own identity, its own language, still spoken in pockets. Go into a good Corsican restaurant in Corsica and they may speak Corsican to you; I have had this experience. But it is not a language widely spoken anymore. It has been completely subsumed by French, and France holds Corsica tightly today. And what is France? To a great extent, it is the creature of a great Corsican named Napoleon Bonaparte, who built the French Empire. Nobody concludes from this that Corsica was not a colony.
It is remarkable to me that Putin still does this. He puts people with Ukrainian backgrounds into key positions—in the military, in propaganda, in negotiations.
- Vladimir Medinsky, one of his chief propagandists and now his negotiator, was born in Smila, in Cherkasy Oblast, my own small motherland.
- Valentina Matviyenko, third in the official hierarchy, comes from Shepetivka in Khmelnytskyi Oblast.
- Kirill Dmitriev, who negotiates with the Americans, was born in Kyiv to a family of Ukrainian biologists.
It was Medinsky, incidentally, who announced in a 2012 interview that the Russian people has one extra chromosome—his explanation for how Russia survived the catastrophes of the twentieth century when other nations, the Scythians and Sarmatians among them, broke and vanished. Russians mocked him for it, since an extra chromosome is the marker of Down syndrome.
As a claim, though, it is a race claim. Made by a man born in Cherkasy Oblast, about a people he was not born into.
They contribute to the Russian neo-empire. They contribute to it not as Ukrainians but as those who denounced Ukrainian identity. This is how empire functions. It absorbs the representatives of subaltern nations who willingly denounce their own will. It was so under the Romanovs. It was so in the Soviet empire. It is so in Putin's quasi-empire now.
Ukrainians were, and still are, a subaltern nation.
Papua, and Scotland
There are worse outcomes than ours and there are better ones.
The Papuans of West Papua tried. They fought for independence, failed, and many of them were killed. They are still oppressed. That is the bad end of the range, and it is not hypothetical.
The better scenario would be the Scots. They had statehood, and it was strong—kings and queens, pride, history, narratives, everything a full and self-sufficient nation possesses. Then they lost it. They are not being killed. They do not suffer the way the Papuans suffer. And yet many of them remain deeply dissatisfied with what they are. We support the United Kingdom, of course, but we are also mindful of the peoples who constitute it—Scots, Irish, Welsh. They have their pride, their nation, their language, their history, their self-consciousness, their identity.
They cannot fully live any of it without independence.
That would be a much better scenario for us than the Papuan one. From where we are now, I still do not think it would be enough.
Colonies taken by neighbors
Timor-Leste has stayed with me. One of the newest countries in the world, independent since 2002, and before that a genocide. Up to a third of its population died. Its capital, Dili, was destroyed in 1999.
Our own Baturyn, the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate, was destroyed by Peter I's army in 1708 in the same way.
And Timor is not an overseas colony. That is the other thing. There is the colonization conducted across an ocean—the Dutch in the Malay Archipelago, to which Timor belongs—and there is the colonization conducted by a neighbor. Indonesia, having been a Dutch colony itself, became independent, developed a colonial attitude within thirty years, and invaded Timor.
Ukraine was taken by neighbors too. First Poland, then the Russian Empire. Both committed atrocities here. We always resisted, and always with some violence—there has never been an anti-colonial struggle that was not violent, and ours is not an exception. I wish it were an exception. It was not.
The first colonization, and the first decolonization
The Polish colonization is the one Ukrainians forget, and it matters for a reason that has nothing to do with Poland.
It ended. And the decolonization from it was successful: we regained our ground, re-established Ukrainian identity on our territory, our own way of living. And there was a process of reconciliation that worked, at least to some extent. That is the first decolonization Ukrainians ever accomplished, and it is the paradigm I hold onto when I think about what happens with Russia.
Which does not mean it is finished. Some of the reactions coming from the Polish side now are, to me, surprising and incomprehensible, and I can explain them only through this lens: post-colonial phantom pain. They lost a limb and they still feel it. Russia feels the same phantom pain about what it calls the Russian World, and reacts far more violently, because Russia is historically far more violent. But the pain is the same kind of pain.
One white nation killing another
Much of the world does not accept that any of this is decolonization. In the Global South the response is: one white nation is killing another white nation, why should we care.
They should care, because our struggle is the same as theirs was. If ours is meaningless, then theirs was meaningless too.
They are working with a black and white colonial paradigm—sometimes literally—which skims over the surface. There is a name for what we are: a South within the North. Inside the Global North pockets of land and people exist whose experience and self-perception are closer to the peoples of the Global South than to their neighbors. Ukraine is one of those pockets. Our vision of ourselves may be nearer to the Global South than to Europe.
Race is the real difference, and I will not pretend otherwise. Though even there the resemblance is closer than people assume. When we were a Polish colony, the Poles developed the idea that we were an inferior people—chłopy—while they were Sarmatians, a superior nation. Not race as skin color. Race as ethnic origin, which does the same work.
By my own study, something like 90% of the criteria that apply to other colonies apply to Ukraine. Perhaps 10% do not.
But before the world can see this, we Ukrainians have to see it.
Why the blood
Fanon believed that violence is embedded in colonialism—that it is intrinsic, that you cannot be a colonial power without being violent, without being prepared to kill the subalterns. He also believed that anticolonial struggle is inevitably violent. Sartre, who wrote the preface to him, believed it too. Maybe that is right, and it would be a good and easy explanation.
But our struggle is particularly bloody for a particular reason, and it is Russian. Russia has adopted most of its ideas from the West, and has almost always put them into practice through violence exceeding anything done in the place the idea came from. Marxist ideas about the counter-revolutionary nature of the peasantry produced the Holodomor; American culture wars are producing this one.
Our resistance is violent because their aggression is. It is a reaction, and it does not exceed the action. If anything it is disproportionate in the other direction. They kill our civilians in daylight and destroy hospitals and residential buildings. We destroy their oil plants and the warehouses of their online marketplaces.
From the standpoint of genocide studies, what is being done to us is a classical genocide. Not a rhetorical trope—a scientifically provable case. What is unprecedented is not the death toll but the intensity: the quantity of weaponry and ammunition involved in this anti-colonial war has no precedent among anti-colonial wars.
Agency
This is what Ukraine has to contribute to postcolonial theory, and I think it is the important thing.
The victims are not powerless and they are not will-less. They have their own volition. They have their own agency. And the purpose of an anti-colonial struggle is to regain agency—not merely independence, not merely economic freedom, not merely the cutting of ties with international capital or with the old and new empires. Agency.
Our struggle is a struggle for and through our agency. And it is a path that other peoples still living with the residues of colonialism could follow.
The neocolonialism that is not Russian
The Russian form is the most obvious available to us. It is not the only one.
The newest arrived with the Trump administration, which tried to exchange support for our resources—rare earth elements and so forth—essentially requiring us to give them up in return for help. This is a classical neocolonial attitude. It is what happens when a neocolonial power is being established.
I want to be careful here, because this is the policy of the White House and not of Americans. Most Americans who come to Ukraine come as volunteers, prepared to sacrifice their lives, because they understand that global democracy depends on what happens here. The neocolonial attitude belongs to a minority. Unfortunately, that minority currently holds power.
It is a new situation for us, but it is not unique for the world. Still, we can survive it if we understand what it is.
Russia is the last European colonial empire, but the West looks away. Expert explains why
Whether it is worth it
It is not for us to answer that.
Our generation has decided that it is worth it. But we should remember that we have also decided for the next generation. The Ukrainian Sich Riflemen, a volunteer legion of students and intelligentsia raised in Lviv in 1914, decided in their time that it was worth sacrificing themselves for Ukrainian independence, and we now judge that they were right. The UPA, fighting into the 1950s, decided the same. They were defeated.
We do not know how the next generation will judge us. Because there will be millions of Ukrainians who will not have been born as a result of this war. They will not decide whether we were right or wrong. They will not exist.
Those who do exist will make the judgment.
Edited by Alya Shandra

articles.title: Khmara discusses strengthening Ukrainian air defense with Wadephul
articles.body:
Khmara discusses strengthening Ukrainian air defense with Wadephul
Ukrinform reported this, citing the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense.
Khmara thanked Germany for its strong and consistent support for Ukraine.
“The key issue is financing Ukraine’s defense. We are counting on Germany to continue playing a leading role in this area,” the defense minister noted. According to him, Germany’s assistance directly affects Ukraine’s ability to protect its troops on the battlefield and civilians in cities.
The sides also discussed strengthening Ukrainian air defense. Khmara emphasized that Germany is already working closely with its partners to strengthen Ukraine’s defense capabilities.
Strengthening air defense remains one of the key priorities for protecting people and critical infrastructure from Russian attacks.
The sides also discussed new joint defense projects. The defense minister emphasized that Ukraine has unique combat experience that can strengthen its partners.
“We will expand mutually beneficial cooperation that will strengthen both Ukraine and Germany,” Khmara assured.
The defense minister thanked Germany and Wadephul personally for their strong and consistent support for Ukraine.
Read also: Ukraine, Germany agree on joint production of BARS drones for Defense Forces
As previsously reported by Ukrinform, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Kharkiv as part of his trip to Ukraine.

articles.title: Kellogg Backs Mobilization of Ukrainian Women
articles.body:
Retired US Lieutenant General and former presidential envoy Keith Kellogg backed the mobilization of women into Ukraine’s Defense Forces, arguing that they can fight as effectively as men.
Speaking with Anna Maksymchuk in an interview posted to Naspravdi MAX’s YouTube channel on Monday, Aug. 24, Kellogg said women’s service should be viewed as part of society’s broader contribution to the war.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Do I think women should be mobilized into the army? My answer is yes, because they fight just as well as men,” Kellogg said.
Women in military service
Citing his own family’s military experience, particularly that of his wife and daughter, Kellogg said he saw no real obstacle to women serving in the military, either personally or professionally.
His daughter reportedly graduated from a US military academy and served in Afghanistan, while his wife served as a paratrooper who took part in combat operations in the Caribbean island of Grenada.
Currently, Ukraine allows women to join the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) voluntarily, while some categories of women – such as those with medical or pharmaceutical qualifications – are required to register for military service, though that does not mean automatic conscription or assignment to combat duties.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian women are increasingly taking on dangerous humanitarian roles, including delivering aid in frontline areas and serving as evacuation medics, as the war has reduced the number of available male volunteers.

Kellogg praises women serving in the AFU
During the conservative international forum, “35 Years of Faith and Freedom,” held in Kyiv on Sunday, Aug. 23, Kellogg praised Ukrainian women already serving in the military.
“Women who serve in the infantry, as snipers, drone operators, medics, and commanders – more than 60,000 members of the AFU – are overcoming barriers and proving that courage has no gender,” Kellogg said, according to a Shelter correspondent.
He also praised Ukrainian veterans as “the living embodiment of Ukraine’s will to be free,” adding that they would remain central to the country’s postwar recovery when they return to regular civilian life.
Kellogg urged Ukraine to provide them proper medical care, psychological support, and fair reintegration, warning that “a nation that forgets its defenders and heroes forgets itself.”
Pence also attends forum
According to Ukrinform, former US Vice President Mike Pence also attended the forum, which aimed to promote and strengthen traditional Western values – “including faith in God, respect for freedom, security, and private property.”
He recalled the Soviet Union “collapsed under the weight of its corruption and oppression,” adding that the world had learned a lesson from that experience.
“The final word does not belong to the tyrant – it belongs to God,” he said, according to Ukrinform.
The forum also saw the launch of the “Faith and Freedom Center,” a think tank intended to develop documents and recommendations on applying conservative approaches to Ukraine’s reconstruction.
It will serve as a platform for engagement with Western conservatives, Ukrinform reported.

articles.title: Russia’s first gasoline purchase from Turkey will be delivered by a shadow fleet tanker
articles.body:
For the first time, Russia has purchased a shipment of gasoline from Turkey, analytics firm S&P Global Commodities at Sea (CAS) reports. A batch of 200,000 barrels will be delivered by the tanker Wendrix (IMO: 9299886), which departed from the port of Mersin on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The gasoline’s manufacturer is unknown.
According to data from Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the Wendrix left Mersin on July 31 and as of Aug. 23 is in the Gulf of Finland, reportedly heading for the Primorsk marine oil terminal in Leningrad Region. The tanker, which sails under the flag of Equatorial Guinea, is part of the “shadow fleet.” The Wendrix (formerly known as the Jasper) is on the sanctions lists of the EU, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, and Switzerland.
The delivery marks the fifth known gasoline shipment to Russia since the start of July. According to CAS and Kpler data, Russia has already received three tankers carrying gasoline originally loaded at a refinery in Vadinar, India, and delivered to Russia after transshipment in Egypt. Another batch came from Morocco (a country that has no operational oil refineries). Analysts estimate the total volume of seaborne gasoline deliveries to Russia during this period at more than 1 million barrels.
On Aug. 22, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told a United Russia congress that gasoline supplies to the domestic market are expected to increase. He said that several oil refineries have completed maintenance and resumed production. However, in order to cover the shortfall, Novak identified imports and the production of gasoline of environmental classes K2, K3 and K4 — which are of lower quality than the Euro-5 standard.
Russia’s fuel crisis, which began in May, saw another rise in intensity earlier this month. Between Aug. 10 and 15, at least six Russian regions reinstated or tightened restrictions on gasoline sales, and the Novosibirsk Region signed the country’s first agreement capping the retail markup on fuel. In July, officials declared that the crisis was easing — but a new wave of strikes on oil processing facilities, including the complete shutdown of the Orsk refinery, largely reversed that progress.

articles.title: Russian drones are entering Moldovan territory due to insufficient support for Ukraine — Sandu
articles.body:
Russian drones are entering Moldovan territory due to insufficient support for Ukraine — Sandu
Kyiv • UNN
Maia Sandu linked the violation of Moldova’s airspace to a lack of assistance to Ukraine in intercepting drones. According to her, Russia deliberately sent a drone at least once.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu said that the frequent violations of her country's airspace by Russian drones are linked to insufficient support for Ukraine to intercept them; however, according to her, there have been cases when Russia deliberately directed drones into Moldovan territory, UNN reports.
"Moldova is seeing an increase in the number of violations of our airspace, especially this year. We believe that one of the reasons is insufficient support for Ukraine to intercept and destroy these drones," Sandu said.
She noted that in at least one case, Russia directed a drone specifically toward Moldova, rather than it having gone off course.
"This was not simply because it had flown from Ukrainian territory. Moldova has invested in intelligence operations in recent years. We have a better ability to see what is happening. We share all the information. But, of course, when it comes directly to countering these threats, the situation is somewhat more complicated, as we need to make significant investments," Sandu added.
We remind you
In Moldova, authorities reported three drone incidents amid Russia's nighttime attack on Ukraine; experts from the country's Interior Ministry examined drone debris found near Giurgiulești, while Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the Russian strikes and said that Russia must face significantly stronger pressure.

articles.title: Explainer-What are Iran's options to escalate further in face of US economic threats?
articles.body:
Explainer-What are Iran's options to escalate further in face of US economic threats?
LONDON, Aug 24 - U.S. threats to impose "the toughest sanctions in history" to force Iran to buckle to its demands after nearly six months of war have raised the prospect of a new round of escalation in the Gulf.
How could Iran respond to the economic pressure?
CAN IRAN STOP MORE OIL GETTING OUT OF THE MIDDLE EAST?
Mohsen Rezaei, the former Revolutionary Guards chief and secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has already threatened to shut down oil exports — one of Tehran's main strategic approaches since the war began on February 28.
"If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf," he said.
Iranian attacks and threats to shipping have already stopped most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, largely shutting down a waterway that carried around a fifth of global energy before the conflict.
Although some oil tankers have been moving through the strait in recent weeks, volumes remain very low and on Sunday Iran blacklisted 45 tankers it says failed to comply with the rules it wants to impose on Hormuz shipping.
Missile, drone or speedboat attacks on tankers trying to leave the Gulf have repeatedly pushed up oil prices during the six months of the conflict.
Meanwhile, Tehran's Houthi allies have restricted Red Sea shipping with attacks and threats to blockade all Saudi Arabian shipping, which carries crude to Asia through the Bab el-Mandeb strait past the group's Yemeni stronghold.
While the attacks initially only stopped some vessels, with more than half still getting through in mid-August, the situation is difficult for shippers with Chinese shipping companies now rerouting away from Bab el-Mandeb, according to industry sources.
Further attacks, such as the one that targeted a vessel off the main Saudi Red Sea oil terminal at Yanbu on Monday or a drone strike near the Suez Canal in early August, could raise oil market anxiety levels and crude oil prices.
ARE GULF STATES STILL AT RISK OF IRANIAN ATTACK?
Iran has threatened to retaliate against any neighbours who take part in U.S. efforts to strangle the country's economy with "earthquake" force.
It has targeted Gulf states and Jordan repeatedly during the war, mostly focusing on U.S. bases but also hitting energy infrastructure and other targets.
Any intensified attacks that targeted upstream oil or gas facilities could further drive up energy prices in ways that inflict political damage on the Trump administration and could be harder to reverse than attacks on shipping.
Targeting power and water desalination plants in the hot, parched region would also pose a major risk to U.S.-aligned Gulf monarchies that function as significant financial hubs for the global economy.
CAN IRAN ATTACK WESTERN COUNTRIES DIRECTLY?
While Western countries are beyond the range of Iran's main munitions, the Revolutionary Guards have historically been willing to find alternative ways of attack.
On Monday, Britain said Iran-linked hackers had shut down a small electricity station while U.S. officials have said Tehran was likely behind cyber attacks on water plants in Minnesota. Iran has not commented on those allegations.
Western security services have also accused Iran of recruiting local people to stage attacks or attempt assassinations in the West. Iran has denied that. REUTERS

articles.title: Qalibaf tells Asim Munir: US bad faith hinders regional stability
articles.body:
Qalibaf tells Asim Munir: US bad faith hinders regional stability
TEHRAN — Pakistan’s Chief of Defense Forces (CDF), Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, held talks with senior Iranian officials, including Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, in Tehran on Monday.
During the meeting, Qalibaf pointed to the US failure to honor its commitments under the memorandum of understanding President Donald Trump signed with Iran on June 17.
“The commitments made by both sides under the memorandum of understanding are clear. It was the United States’ failure to honor its commitments that undermined regional stability and gave us yet another reason not to trust Washington,” Qalibaf said.
Munir, for his part, said he would continue efforts to help restore regional peace. He arrived in Iran earlier on Monday.
The Pakistani-mediated MoU established framework terms to cease hostilities. While subsequent US aerial strikes and naval blockades disrupted the agreement, Pakistan had already demonstrated its diplomatic role by helping facilitate the April 8 ceasefire that paused the 39-day war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28.
Tehran has repeatedly expressed its gratitude to Pakistan for its diplomatic support and conflict-resolution efforts during critical moments of crisis.  Beyond defense cooperation, economic partnership remains central to their bilateral relationship. Under comprehensive joint agreements, Tehran and Islamabad are actively expanding cross-border infrastructure, trade market access, and energy links. These initiatives aim to scale bilateral trade volume from over $3 billion to a targeted $10 billion, reflecting a mutual commitment to leveraging shared geography for long-term economic integration and regional peace.

articles.title: US launches ‘economic D-Day’ against Iran, threatens sanctions on its global partners
articles.body:
ALBAWABA- The United States on Monday launched what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described as an “economic D-Day” against Iran, unveiling a sweeping campaign designed to cut Tehran off from international financial networks and choke the revenues sustaining its government and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Bessent warned that no country, company or financial institution would be beyond the reach of US sanctions. He said Washington would target those helping Iran convert oil into cash, finance the government or IRGC, or facilitate transactions through the international financial system. Any institution found helping Iran launder money could be excluded from the US dollar system.
The campaign includes expanded secondary sanctions against foreign entities dealing with Iran. The Treasury announced measures against nearly 60 individuals and entities, including brokers, companies and vessels linked to Iran’s oil trade and shadow fleet across the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, Singapore, Switzerland, Europe and China. The new measures also focus on Iran-linked activities in digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Bessent also delivered a direct warning to Iran’s trading partners, including China. He said every country would have a defined period to wind down activities identified by Washington, while stressing that the United States would not immediately impose a universal deadline because it wanted countries to have an opportunity to change course. “Our patience is not infinite,” he said.
The campaign comes after nearly six months of US-Iran conflict and amid a broader deadlock over efforts to end the war. Washington has sought to use military and economic pressure to force Tehran to make concessions, while Iran has continued to resist demands for capitulation. The US also faces the difficult task of enforcing secondary sanctions without triggering a major confrontation with China, Iran’s most important trading partner.
Iran’s economy is already under severe pressure. The Iranian rial fell to a record low on Monday, reaching about 2 million rials to the US dollar on the open market, as inflation, disrupted oil exports and the effects of the war intensified economic strain.
Iranian officials have rejected the US strategy, arguing that Washington has imposed sanctions for years without succeeding in collapsing the Iranian economy. Iran’s economic leadership says the country has developed mechanisms to circumvent sanctions and rebuild damaged industries, insisting that the latest US campaign will not sever the “arteries” of the Iranian economy.
Diplomatic activity has meanwhile intensified. Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in Tehran for talks aimed at helping break the deadlock between Iran and the United States. Oman is also pursuing a diplomatic channel. Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi is scheduled to visit Tehran on Tuesday for talks on the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Russia must pay for the war against Ukraine with its frozen assets – Latvian PM

Russia must pay for the war against Ukraine with its frozen assets – Latvian PM
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said this at a press conference following the Coalition of the Willing summit held in Kyiv on August 24, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
The Latvian prime minister noted that Russia is not only waging war against Ukraine but also carrying out hybrid attacks against EU countries. In particular, through illegal migration organized by the Kremlin via Belarus, Russia is testing EU countries’ ability to respond, as well as the speed of their response and their technical capabilities. In addition, Moscow is carrying out cyberattacks in European countries, attempting to destabilize social developments and influence public sentiment.
“I think Russia should start paying for these brutal attacks. And we have to agree to use frozen Russian assets, rather than EU citizens’ money, to pay this bill. It is very high… There are actually €200 billion available that can be used to pay this bill,” Kulbergs said.
He added that the cost of the war unleashed by Russia is enormous for Ukraine, and this burden must be lifted from Ukraine.
“It is easy to do this—we must not allow Russia to make money. And we are allowing it to make money to finance its war spending… Russian LNG is still being purchased, gas supplies from Russia are still continuing, the Strait of Hormuz being blocked provides an additional injection into Russia’s economy. All of this ultimately turns into missiles that fall on Ukrainian soil. This is a bill that must be paid,” the Latvian prime minister emphasized.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Latvia and Ukraine have moved to the practical implementation phase of the Drone Deal in the months since it was signed and are currently addressing three specific issues.

articles.title: Trump moves toward levying new tariff on China for flooding market with cheap goods, AP sources say
articles.body:
Trump moves toward levying new tariff on China for flooding market with cheap goods, AP sources say
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is moving toward levying a new tariff on China that would penalize the world’s second-largest economy for flooding the global market with underpriced goods, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Two of the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations still being finalized, said Trump is considering setting the new tariff at 7.5%. It’s a level administration officials believe would not endanger the one-year trade truce between Washington and Beijing or a planned White House meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to take place in late September.
The move, if finalized, appears to be a calibrated effort by the White House to work around a Supreme Court decision earlier this year that struck down Trump’s plan to implement a sweeping, high-tariff scheme not seen since the 1930s.
After that decision, the Trump administration announced in March it was launching formal investigations targeting excess industrial capacity and forced-labor regulations in China and other nations.
It isn’t clear if the U.S. administration is also nearing its decision in its probes of the other economies that it announced it was investigating for unfair trade practices, including the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India.
The White House and the U.S. Trade Representative’s office did not respond to requests for comment on the tariff deliberations, which Bloomberg News reported earlier Monday.
The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement that economic and trade issues should be resolved through bilateral talks rather than unilateral tariff actions, and rejected the idea that it has an issue with overcapacity.
The excess industrial capacity probe of China was initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against U.S. companies or commerce.
The new tariff would come on top of existing tariffs on China
The people familiar with the deliberations stressed that Trump could still change his mind on the new tariff on China.
It would come on top of tariffs of 10% to 12.5% announced last month for 60 economies around the globe that the Trump administration accused of failing to effectively enforce a ban on goods produced with forced labor.
Many countries, including China, protested that move, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary tariffs Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every U.S. trade partner.
China last month pushed back against claims of overcapacity, anticipating that the U.S. would soon release results of its probe and impose new tariffs.
Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing’s trading partners in recent years.
Although China’s own leaders have prioritized rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China’s trade surplus to a record of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.
China has never sought a large trade surplus, the Ministry of Commerce said in a recently published report titled “China’s Position on the So-called Excess Capacity Issue.”
The deliberations come as the Treasury Department on Monday warned countries doing trade with Iran that new secondary sanctions are in the pipeline aimed at ostracizing nations that continue to do business with Tehran. China is Iran’s biggest trade partner.
Washington has promised the new sanctions would put even more pressure on an Iranian economy already battered by previous sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade as the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran nears the six-month mark.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement Monday provided little detail and did not name which countries could face secondary sanctions.
___
AP writer Paul Wiseman contributed reporting.

articles.title: Russia and China expand trade via Arctic sea route
articles.body:
Russia and China expand trade via Arctic sea route
Russia and China have expanded trade links through the Arctic, with the first Chinese container ship arriving at Russia’s northern port of Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route (NSR), Rosatom announced on Monday. Beijing has described the growing cooperation with Moscow as part of its “Ice Silk Road” initiative.
The NSR runs through Russia’s Arctic waters and exclusive economic zone, relying on Russian ports and icebreakers. State atomic energy corporation Rosatom oversees the route’s development, navigation, infrastructure and maritime safety.
NewNew Shipping Line’s Xin Xin Hai 1 arrived in Murmansk on Wednesday carrying 500 containers of automotive components, Rosatom said.
“This was the first container ship from China to arrive at the Murmansk Commercial Sea Port,” the corporation said.
NewNew Shipping Line has operated along the NSR since 2023, although its vessels have previously generally carried cargo to ports in Russia’s Far East or the Baltic.
China is ready to continue “playing the role of a bridge” to support cooperation between Chinese companies and the Murmansk Region and further develop the “Ice Silk Road,” Chinese Consul General in St. Petersburg Luo Zhanhui said on Thursday.
Earlier this month, NewNew Shipping Line CEO Ke Jin announced plans to deploy six new Arctic-class container ships on the NSR, each capable of carrying around 4,800 standard containers. Four are due to enter service in October, enabling two voyages a month between Chinese and Russian ports, with another two expected to join the fleet in June 2027.
Ke has also expressed interest in investing in the ports of Murmansk and Arkhangelsk in Russia’s far north and acquiring a stake in the port of Ust-Luga.
China accounted for around 40% of the Murmansk Region’s foreign trade in 2025, when the region traded with 48 countries, according to Governor Andrey Chibis.
Russia has long used the Arctic corridor for energy exports. LNG shipments from the Yamal LNG project began in 2017, with the first cargoes delivered eastward to China via the NSR the following year. Russia has also shipped other hydrocarbons along the route to Asian markets since 2010.
The Northern Sea Route provides a shorter maritime link between East Asia and northern Europe and can cut around two weeks from a voyage between China and Europe compared with the route through the Suez Canal, according to Rosatom.
Interest in the Arctic corridor has also grown as the US war with Iran and instability in the Middle East have disrupted shipping through the Persian Gulf and Red Sea. South Korea launched its first trial container voyage to Europe via the NSR on Saturday, while India plans to send its first cargo ship along the route in 2027.

Munir also met in Tehran with Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, as well as Mohsen Rezaei, head of the country’s highest national security body, according to Iranian state television.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Aug 24 laid out plans for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, expanding Washington’s secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign. AFP

articles.title: Over 50 UN member states call on Russia to agree to full, unconditional ceasefire in Ukraine
articles.body:
Over 50 UN member states call on Russia to agree to full, unconditional ceasefire in Ukraine
The appeal was made in a joint statement read out by Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen ahead of Monday’s UN Security Council meeting, an Ukrinform correspondent reports from New York.
“Today, Ukraine marks its Independence Day – 35 years since it declared its independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991. This was a decision made by the Ukrainian people and recognized by the international community, including by Russia. Yet, rather than being a day of celebration, today also marks four and a half years since the start of Russia’s illegal full-scale military invasion of Ukraine. A blatant and continuing violation of the UN Charter and of fundamental principles of international law,” the statement reads.
It stressed that Russia’s invasion had “challenged the foundation of the rules-based international order and undermined both regional and global peace and security.”
The signatories noted that hundreds of thousands of men, women and children had been killed or injured as a result of Russian aggression, while civilian casualties had risen sharply amid intensified attacks.
“Last month alone OHCHR recorded the highest number of civilians killed and injured in a single month since May 2022, claiming the lives of at least 437 Ukrainian civilians,” the statement said.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, at least 68,000 Ukrainian civilians have been killed or injured, including nearly 4,000 children.
The countries also highlighted the war’s consequences beyond Ukraine, including violations of European airspace and drone incidents in European countries.
They condemned Russian attacks on Ukrainian shipping and port infrastructure in the Black Sea, saying these attacks have serious implications for global food security.
“This senseless war and the immense human suffering could end immediately. Russia simply needs to accept the unconditional ceasefire that Ukraine and the international community has been calling for over a year and a half now,” the statement said.
“We strongly urge Russia to respond to the calls for a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire and resume talks for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with international law, including the UN Charter,” the document said.
The signatories also reaffirmed their support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.
“On this special day, we will continue to stand firmly by Ukraine. There is no alternative to a just and lasting peace in accordance with the UN Charter,” the statement said.
The statement was supported by all EU member states, as well as other European countries, Australia, Canada, Costa Rica, Georgia, Honduras, Iceland, Japan, New Zealand, Panama and South Korea.
As reported, European members of the UN Security Council condemned Russia’s occupation of Abkhazia and South Ossetia and called on Moscow to withdraw its forces from Georgian territory.
